In delivering my son from me, I bury a second husband.
In sending my son away from me, I bury a second husband.
And I in going, madam, weep o'er my father's death anew; but I must / attend his majesty's command, to whom I am now in ward, evermore in / subjection.
And in going, madam, I weep for my father's death all over again. But I must obey the King's command. I'm his ward now, and always his subject.

You shall find of the king a husband, madam; you, sir, a father. He / that so generally is at all times good, must of necessity hold his / virtue to you, whose worthiness would stir it up where it wanted, / rather than lack it where there is such abundance.

You'll find the King a husband to you, madam, and a father to you, sir. He is good to everyone at all times, so he's bound to be good to you. Your own worth would bring out his goodness even if he lacked it, and there's no lack of it in him.
What hope is there of his majesty's amendment?
What hope is there of the King getting better?
He hath abandon'd his physicians, madam; under whose practices he hath / persecuted time with hope, and finds no other advantage in the process / but only the losing of hope by time.
He has given up his doctors, madam. Under their treatment he has spent his time hoping, and all he has gained from it is losing hope as time goes on.

This young gentlewoman had a father—O that "had!", how sad a passage / 'tis!—whose skill was almost as great as his honesty; had it stretch'd / so far, would have made nature immortal, and death should have play for / lack of work. Would for the king's sake he were living! I think it / would be the death of the king's disease.

This young lady had a father (oh, that "had"! What a sad word it is!) whose skill was almost as great as his honesty. If it had stretched that far, it would have made people immortal, and Death would have had nothing to do. I wish for the King's sake he were alive! I think he would have been the death of the King's disease.
How called you the man you speak of, madam?
What was the man's name, madam?
He was famous, sir, in his profession, and it was his great right to be / so: Gerard de Narbon.
He was famous in his profession, sir, and he deserved to be: Gerard de Narbon.
He was excellent indeed, madam; the king very lately spoke of him / admiringly, and mourningly; he was skilful enough to have liv'd still, / if knowledge could be set up against mortality.
He was excellent indeed, madam. The King spoke of him only recently, with admiration and with grief. He was skilful enough to be living still, if knowledge could hold out against death.
What is it, my good lord, the king languishes of?
What illness is the King wasting away from, my lord?
I heard not of it before.
I hadn't heard of it before.
I would it were not notorious. Was this gentlewoman the daughter of / Gerard de Narbon?
I wish it weren't common knowledge. Was this young lady Gerard de Narbon's daughter?

His sole child, my lord, and bequeathed to my overlooking. I have those / hopes of her good that her education promises her dispositions she / inherits, which makes fair gifts fairer; for where an unclean mind / carries virtuous qualities, there commendations go with pity, they are / virtues and traitors too. In her they are the better for their / simpleness; she derives her honesty, and achieves her goodness.

His only child, my lord, and left in my care. I expect great good of her, because her upbringing adds to the nature she was born with, and that makes fine gifts finer. When someone with a corrupt mind has good abilities, praise comes mixed with regret: those abilities are virtues and traitors at once. In her they are all the better for being pure. Her honesty she inherits; her goodness she earns.
Your commendations, madam, get from her tears.
Your praise brings tears to her eyes, madam.

'Tis the best brine a maiden can season her praise in. The remembrance / of her father never approaches her heart but the tyranny of her sorrows / takes all livelihood from her cheek. No more of this, Helena; go to, no / more, lest it be rather thought you affect a sorrow than to have.

Tears are the best salt a young woman can preserve her praise in. Whenever she remembers her father, her grief is so cruel that it drains all the life from her face. No more of this, Helena. Come on, no more, or people will think you are putting on a sorrow rather than really feeling one.
I do affect a sorrow indeed, but I have it too.
I do put on a sorrow, but I really feel one too.
Moderate lamentation is the right of the dead; excessive grief the / enemy to the living.
Moderate grief is what the dead deserve. Too much grief is the enemy of the living.
If the living be enemy to the grief, the excess makes it soon mortal.
If the living fight against grief, too much of it soon kills itself off.
Madam, I desire your holy wishes.
Madam, I ask for your blessing.
What does he mean by that?

Be thou blest, Bertram, and succeed thy father / In manners, as in shape! Thy blood and virtue / Contend for empire in thee, and thy goodness / Share with thy birthright! Love all, trust a few, / Do wrong to none. Be able for thine enemy / Rather in power than use; and keep thy friend / Under thy own life's key. Be check'd for silence, / But never tax'd for speech. What heaven more will, / That thee may furnish and my prayers pluck down, / Fall on thy head! Farewell. My lord, / 'Tis an unseason'd courtier; good my lord, / Advise him.

Bless you, Bertram, and may you be like your father in behaviour as you are in looks! May your noble blood and your goodness compete to rule you, and may your virtue match your birth! Love everyone, trust only a few, and do wrong to no one. Be strong enough to beat your enemy, but don't use that strength. Guard your friend as closely as your own life. Be told off for keeping quiet, but never blamed for what you say. Whatever else heaven wants to give you, and my prayers can bring down, may it fall on your head! Goodbye. My lord, he's an inexperienced courtier. Please, my lord, advise him.
He cannot want the best / That shall attend his love.
He won't lack the best advice my love can give him.
The best wishes that can be forg'd in your thoughts be servants to you! / [To Helena] Be comfortable to my mother, your mistress, and make / much of her.
May the best wishes you can think of serve you well! [To Helena] Look after my mother, your mistress, and take good care of her.
Farewell, pretty lady, you must hold the credit of your father.
Goodbye, pretty lady. You must live up to your father's good name.

O, were that all! I think not on my father, / And these great tears grace his remembrance more / Than those I shed for him. What was he like? / I have forgot him; my imagination / Carries no favour in't but Bertram's. / I am undone: there is no living, none, / If Bertram be away. 'Twere all one / That I should love a bright particular star, / And think to wed it, he is so above me. / In his bright radiance and collateral light / Must I be comforted, not in his sphere. / Th'ambition in my love thus plagues itself: / The hind that would be mated by the lion / Must die for love. 'Twas pretty, though a plague, / To see him every hour; to sit and draw / His arched brows, his hawking eye, his curls, / In our heart's table,—heart too capable / Of every line and trick of his sweet favour. / But now he's gone, and my idolatrous fancy / Must sanctify his relics. Who comes here?

If only that were all! I'm not thinking about my father, and these big tears honour his memory more than the ones I actually shed for him. What did he look like? I've forgotten him. My imagination holds no face but Bertram's. I'm ruined: there's no living, none at all, if Bertram is away. I might as well love one bright star in the sky and think of marrying it, he is so far above me. I must take comfort in his light shining on me from a distance, not in sharing his sphere. My ambitious love torments itself: the deer that wants to mate with the lion must die of love. It was sweet, though it was torture, to see him every hour, to sit and draw his arched eyebrows, his keen hawk-like eyes and his curls on the drawing board of my heart, a heart that took in every line and feature of his lovely face. But now he's gone, and my love, which worships him like an idol, must treat the things he left behind as holy relics. Who's this coming?

One that goes with him: I love him for his sake, / And yet I know him a notorious liar, / Think him a great way fool, solely a coward; / Yet these fix'd evils sit so fit in him / That they take place when virtue's steely bones / Looks bleak i' th' cold wind: withal, full oft we see / Cold wisdom waiting on superfluous folly.

One of the men going with him. I love him for Bertram's sake, and yet I know he's a notorious liar, I think he's mostly a fool, and he's nothing but a coward. Yet these rooted faults suit him so well that they find a welcome, while virtue, with its hard bones, is left shivering out in the cold wind. Very often we see cold wisdom serving showy foolishness.
Ay. You have some stain of soldier in you; let me ask you a question. / Man is enemy to virginity; how may we barricado it against him?
Yes. You have a touch of the soldier about you, so let me ask you a question. Man is the enemy of virginity. How can we barricade it against him?
But he assails; and our virginity, though valiant, in the defence, yet / is weak. Unfold to us some warlike resistance.
But he attacks, and our virginity, though it is brave, is weak in defending itself. Show us some military way to resist.
There is none. Man setting down before you will undermine you and blow / you up.
There isn't one. A man who lays siege to you will dig under your walls and blow you up.
Bless our poor virginity from underminers and blowers-up! Is there no / military policy how virgins might blow up men?
God protect our poor virginity from diggers and blowers-up! Is there no military plan by which virgins might blow men up?

Virginity being blown down, man will quicklier be blown up; marry, in / blowing him down again, with the breach yourselves made, you lose your / city. It is not politic in the commonwealth of nature to preserve / virginity. Loss of virginity is rational increase, and there was never / virgin got till virginity was first lost. That you were made of is / metal to make virgins. Virginity, by being once lost, may be ten times / found; by being ever kept, it is ever lost. 'Tis too cold a companion. / Away with it!

Once virginity is blown down, a man will quickly be blown up (made proud and swollen). But when you blow him down again, through the breach you've made yourselves, you lose your city. It isn't good policy in nature's state to keep virginity. Losing virginity leads to a sensible increase, and no virgin was ever conceived until virginity was first lost. What you were made of is the stuff for making virgins. Virginity, once lost, can be found ten times over; kept for ever, it is lost for ever. It's too cold a companion. Get rid of it!
I will stand for't a little, though therefore I die a virgin.
I'll defend it a little longer, even if that means I die a virgin.

There's little can be said in't; 'tis against the rule of nature. To / speak on the part of virginity is to accuse your mothers; which is most / infallible disobedience. He that hangs himself is a virgin: virginity / murders itself, and should be buried in highways out of all sanctified / limit, as a desperate offendress against nature. Virginity breeds / mites, much like a cheese; consumes itself to the very paring, and so / dies with feeding his own stomach. Besides, virginity is peevish, / proud, idle, made of self-love, which is the most inhibited sin in the / canon. Keep it not; you cannot choose but lose by't. Out with't! Within / the year it will make itself two, which is a goodly increase, and the / principal itself not much the worse. Away with it!

There's little to be said for it; it's against the law of nature. To speak up for virginity is to accuse your own mothers, which is outright disobedience. A virgin is like a man who hangs himself: virginity murders itself, and should be buried at a crossroads outside holy ground, as a desperate offender against nature. Virginity breeds mites, just like a cheese; it eats itself away to the rind, and so it dies from feeding on itself. Besides, virginity is bad-tempered, proud, idle and made of self-love, which is the most forbidden sin in the Church's law. Don't keep it; you can only lose by it. Out with it! Within a year it will turn into two, which is a fine profit, and the original investment won't be much the worse. Get rid of it!
How might one do, sir, to lose it to her own liking?
How might a woman lose it, sir, in a way she would like?

Let me see. Marry, ill, to like him that ne'er it likes. 'Tis a / commodity will lose the gloss with lying; the longer kept, the less / worth. Off with't while 'tis vendible; answer the time of request. / Virginity, like an old courtier, wears her cap out of fashion, richly / suited, but unsuitable, just like the brooch and the toothpick, which / wear not now. Your date is better in your pie and your porridge than in / your cheek. And your virginity, your old virginity, is like one of our / French wither'd pears; it looks ill, it eats drily; marry, 'tis a / wither'd pear; it was formerly better; marry, yet 'tis a wither'd pear. / Will you anything with it?

Let me see. Well, by doing wrong and liking a man who doesn't like virginity. It's a product that loses its shine the longer it sits on the shelf; the longer it's kept, the less it's worth. Sell it while it's still saleable; meet the demand while it lasts. Virginity is like an old courtier who wears an old-fashioned hat: richly dressed but out of style, like the brooch and the toothpick, which nobody wears any more. A date is better in your pie and your porridge than in your cheek. And your virginity, your old virginity, is like one of our French withered pears: it looks bad and tastes dry. Yes, it's a withered pear. It used to be better, but it's still a withered pear. Do you want to do anything with it?

Not my virginity yet. / There shall your master have a thousand loves, / A mother, and a mistress, and a friend, / A phoenix, captain, and an enemy, / A guide, a goddess, and a sovereign, / A counsellor, a traitress, and a dear: / His humble ambition, proud humility, / His jarring concord, and his discord dulcet, / His faith, his sweet disaster; with a world / Of pretty, fond, adoptious christendoms / That blinking Cupid gossips. Now shall he— / I know not what he shall. God send him well! / The court's a learning-place; and he is one.

Not with my virginity yet. At court your master will find a thousand loves: a mother, a mistress and a friend, a phoenix, a captain and an enemy, a guide, a goddess and a ruler, an adviser, a traitor and a darling; his humble ambition and proud humility, his clashing harmony and sweet discord, his faith and his sweet disaster, and a whole world of pretty, foolish pet names that blind Cupid gives out. Now he will... I don't know what he will. God keep him well! The court is a place for learning, and he is one...
One I wish well. It's a pity...

That wishing well had not a body in't / Which might be felt, that we, the poorer born, / Whose baser stars do shut us up in wishes, / Might with effects of them follow our friends, / And show what we alone must think, which never / Returns us thanks.

That wishing well has no body that can be felt. Then we who are born poor, whose lowly stars shut us up in mere wishes, might follow our friends with real actions, and show them what we can only think, which never earns us any thanks.
Monsieur Parolles, my lord calls for you.
Monsieur Parolles, my lord is calling for you.
Little Helen, farewell. If I can remember thee, I will think of thee at / court.
Goodbye, little Helen. If I can remember you, I'll think of you at court.
Monsieur Parolles, you were born under a charitable star.
Monsieur Parolles, you were born under a kindly star.
I really do think so: under Mars.
The wars hath so kept you under, that you must needs be born under / Mars.
The wars have kept you so far under that you must have been born under Mars.
When Mars was at his strongest.
When he was retrograde, I think rather.
When he was going backwards, I think.
You go so much backward when you fight.
You go backwards so much when you fight.
So is running away, when fear proposes the safety: but the composition / that your valour and fear makes in you is a virtue of a good wing, and / I like the wear well.
So is running away, when fear says it's safer. But the mixture of courage and fear in you is a quality that gives you good wings, and I like the way it suits you.

I am so full of business I cannot answer thee acutely. I will return / perfect courtier; in the which my instruction shall serve to naturalize / thee, so thou wilt be capable of a courtier's counsel, and understand / what advice shall thrust upon thee; else thou diest in thine / unthankfulness, and thine ignorance makes thee away. Farewell. When / thou hast leisure, say thy prayers; when thou hast none, remember thy / friends. Get thee a good husband, and use him as he uses thee. So, / farewell.

I'm so busy I can't give you a sharp answer. I'll come back a perfect courtier, and then my teaching will make you a native of the court, if you're able to take a courtier's advice and understand what's urged on you. Otherwise you'll die ungrateful, and your ignorance will finish you off. Goodbye. When you have time, say your prayers; when you don't, remember your friends. Get yourself a good husband, and treat him as he treats you. So, goodbye.

Our remedies oft in ourselves do lie, / Which we ascribe to heaven: the fated sky / Gives us free scope; only doth backward pull / Our slow designs when we ourselves are dull. / What power is it which mounts my love so high, / That makes me see, and cannot feed mine eye? / The mightiest space in fortune nature brings / To join like likes, and kiss like native things. / Impossible be strange attempts to those / That weigh their pains in sense, and do suppose / What hath been cannot be. Who ever strove / To show her merit that did miss her love? / The king's disease,—my project may deceive me, / But my intents are fix'd, and will not leave me.

The cures we look to heaven for are often inside ourselves. The stars give us freedom to act; they only hold back our plans when we ourselves are slow. What power is it that lifts my love so high, that lets me see what I want but never have it? Nature can bring together things separated by the greatest distance of fortune, and make them join and kiss as if they were born equals. Strange attempts seem impossible only to those who measure the effort by common sense and assume that what has never happened can't happen. What woman who tried to show her worth ever failed to win her love? The King's disease... my plan may let me down, but my mind is made up, and it won't leave me.
The Florentines and Senoys are by th' ears; / Have fought with equal fortune, and continue / A braving war.
The Florentines and the Sienese are at each other's throats. They've fought with equal luck, and the war of defiance goes on.

Nay, 'tis most credible, we here receive it, / A certainty, vouch'd from our cousin Austria, / With caution, that the Florentine will move us / For speedy aid; wherein our dearest friend / Prejudicates the business, and would seem / To have us make denial.

No, it's entirely believable. We've received it here as a certainty, confirmed by our cousin the Duke of Austria, along with a warning that the Duke of Florence will ask us for quick help. In this our dearest friend has judged the matter in advance and seems to want us to refuse.
His love and wisdom, / Approv'd so to your majesty, may plead / For amplest credence.
His love and wisdom, so well proven to your majesty, deserve your fullest trust.
He hath arm'd our answer, / And Florence is denied before he comes: / Yet, for our gentlemen that mean to see / The Tuscan service, freely have they leave / To stand on either part.
He has armed our answer for us: Florence is refused before he even asks. Still, any of our gentlemen who want to see service in Tuscany are free to fight on either side.
It well may serve / A nursery to our gentry, who are sick / For breathing and exploit.
It may well serve as a training ground for our young noblemen, who are longing for exercise and action.
It is the Count Rossillon, my good lord, / Young Bertram.
It is the Count of Rossillon, my good lord, young Bertram.
Youth, thou bear'st thy father's face; / Frank nature, rather curious than in haste, / Hath well compos'd thee. Thy father's moral parts / Mayst thou inherit too! Welcome to Paris.
Young man, you have your father's face. Generous nature took care rather than hurry when she made you, and made you well. May you inherit your father's good character too! Welcome to Paris.
My thanks and duty are your majesty's.
My thanks and my duty belong to your majesty.

I would I had that corporal soundness now, / As when thy father and myself in friendship / First tried our soldiership. He did look far / Into the service of the time, and was / Discipled of the bravest. He lasted long, / But on us both did haggish age steal on, / And wore us out of act. It much repairs me / To talk of your good father; in his youth / He had the wit which I can well observe / Today in our young lords; but they may jest / Till their own scorn return to them unnoted / Ere they can hide their levity in honour / So like a courtier, contempt nor bitterness / Were in his pride or sharpness; if they were, / His equal had awak'd them, and his honour, / Clock to itself, knew the true minute when / Exception bid him speak, and at this time / His tongue obey'd his hand. Who were below him / He us'd as creatures of another place, / And bow'd his eminent top to their low ranks, / Making them proud of his humility, / In their poor praise he humbled. Such a man / Might be a copy to these younger times; / Which, followed well, would demonstrate them now / But goers backward.

I wish I were as healthy in body now as I was when your father and I, as friends, first tried our hand at soldiering. He understood the warfare of the time deeply, and he learned from the bravest. He lasted a long time, but ugly old age crept up on us both and wore us out of action. It does me a lot of good to talk about your fine father. In his youth he had the wit I can see today in our young lords, but they can go on joking until their mockery comes back on them unnoticed, before they can cover their lightness with honour. He was such a true courtier that there was no contempt or bitterness in his pride or his sharpness. If there was, it was only because an equal had provoked it. His sense of honour, like a clock, knew the exact minute when an objection called on him to speak, and then his tongue obeyed his hand. People below him he treated as if they came from a higher rank, and bowed his great head to their low position, so that they were proud of his humility while he humbled himself by accepting their poor praise. Such a man could be a model for these younger times. If they followed it well, it would show them that they are now only going backwards.
His good remembrance, sir, / Lies richer in your thoughts than on his tomb; / So in approof lives not his epitaph / As in your royal speech.
Your memory of him, sir, is richer than anything on his tomb. His epitaph is not as well proved there as it is in your royal words.

Would I were with him! He would always say,— / Methinks I hear him now; his plausive words / He scatter'd not in ears, but grafted them / To grow there and to bear,—"Let me not live," / This his good melancholy oft began / On the catastrophe and heel of pastime, / When it was out,—"Let me not live" quoth he, / "After my flame lacks oil, to be the snuff / Of younger spirits, whose apprehensive senses / All but new things disdain; whose judgments are / Mere fathers of their garments; whose constancies / Expire before their fashions." This he wish'd. / I, after him, do after him wish too, / Since I nor wax nor honey can bring home, / I quickly were dissolved from my hive / To give some labourers room.

I wish I were with him! He always used to say... I think I can hear him now. He didn't scatter his fine words into people's ears; he planted them there to grow and bear fruit. "Let me not live," his gentle sadness often began, at the end of some entertainment, when it was over. "Let me not live," he said, "after my lamp runs out of oil, to be the snuff-end of younger spirits, whose quick minds scorn anything that isn't new, whose judgements give birth to nothing but new clothes, and whose loyalty dies before their fashions do." That's what he wished. And I, after him, wish the same. Since I can bring home neither wax nor honey, I wish I were quickly removed from my hive to make room for some workers.
You're lov'd, sir; / They that least lend it you shall lack you first.
You're loved, sir. Those who give you least love will be the first to miss you.
I fill a place, I know't. How long is't, Count, / Since the physician at your father's died? / He was much fam'd.
I take up space, I know it. How long is it, Count, since your father's doctor died? He was very famous.
Some six months since, my lord.
About six months ago, my lord.

If he were living, I would try him yet;— / Lend me an arm;—the rest have worn me out / With several applications; nature and sickness / Debate it at their leisure. Welcome, Count; / My son's no dearer.

If he were alive, I would still try him. Give me your arm. The others have worn me out with their different treatments; nature and sickness are left to argue it out at their leisure. Welcome, Count. My own son is no dearer to me.
I will now hear. What say you of this gentlewoman?
Now I'll listen. What do you have to say about this young lady?

Madam, the care I have had to even your content, I wish might be found / in the calendar of my past endeavours; for then we wound our modesty, / and make foul the clearness of our deservings, when of ourselves we / publish them.

Madam, I hope you'll find the care I've taken to please you written down in the record of my past service. We hurt our modesty and spoil the honesty of our good deeds when we advertise them ourselves.

What does this knave here? Get you gone, sirrah. The complaints I have / heard of you I do not all believe; 'tis my slowness that I do not; for / I know you lack not folly to commit them, and have ability enough to / make such knaveries yours.

What's this rogue doing here? Get out, fellow. I don't believe all the complaints I've heard about you. That's my slowness, because I know you're foolish enough to do those things, and clever enough to carry off such tricks.
'Tis not unknown to you, madam, I am a poor fellow.
You know very well, madam, that I'm a poor man.
No, madam, 'tis not so well that I am poor, though many of the rich are / damned; but if I may have your ladyship's good will to go to the world, / Isbel the woman and I will do as we may.
No, madam, it's not so well that I'm poor, though plenty of rich people are damned. But if I may have your ladyship's permission to get married, Isbel the maid and I will do the best we can.
Wilt thou needs be a beggar?
Are you determined to be a beggar?
I do beg your good will in this case.
I do beg your permission in this case.
In Isbel's case and mine own. Service is no heritage, and I think I / shall never have the blessing of God till I have issue of my body; for / they say barnes are blessings.
In Isbel's case and my own. Being a servant is no inheritance, and I don't think I'll have God's blessing until I have children of my own body, because they say children are blessings.
Tell me thy reason why thou wilt marry.
Tell me why you want to marry.
My poor body, madam, requires it; I am driven on by the flesh, and he / must needs go that the devil drives.
My poor body needs it, madam. I'm driven on by the flesh, and a man has to go where the devil drives him.
Is this all your worship's reason?
Is that all the reason your worship has?
Faith, madam, I have other holy reasons, such as they are.
Honestly, madam, I have other holy reasons, such as they are.
I have been, madam, a wicked creature, as you and all flesh and blood / are; and indeed I do marry that I may repent.
I've been a wicked creature, madam, as you and all flesh and blood are, and in fact I'm marrying so that I can repent.
Thy marriage, sooner than thy wickedness.
You'll repent your marriage sooner than your wickedness.
I am out of friends, madam, and I hope to have friends for my wife's / sake.
I've no friends, madam, and I hope to make friends for my wife's sake.
Such friends are thine enemies, knave.
Friends like that are your enemies, you rogue.

Y'are shallow, madam, in great friends; for the knaves come to do that / for me which I am a-weary of. He that ears my land spares my team, and / gives me leave to in the crop: if I be his cuckold, he's my drudge. He / that comforts my wife is the cherisher of my flesh and blood; he that / cherishes my flesh and blood loves my flesh and blood; he that loves my / flesh and blood is my friend; ergo, he that kisses my wife is my / friend. If men could be contented to be what they are, there were no / fear in marriage; for young Charbon the puritan and old Poysam the / papist, howsome'er their hearts are sever'd in religion, their heads / are both one; they may jowl horns together like any deer i' the herd.

You don't understand much about great friends, madam, because those rogues come to do for me the work I'm tired of. The man who ploughs my land saves my horses and lets me bring in the harvest. If he makes me a cuckold, he's my labourer. The man who comforts my wife looks after my flesh and blood; the man who looks after my flesh and blood loves my flesh and blood; the man who loves my flesh and blood is my friend; therefore the man who kisses my wife is my friend. If men could be happy to be what they are, there'd be nothing to fear in marriage. Young Charbon the Puritan and old Poysam the Catholic, however much their hearts are split by religion, have heads that are just the same: they can knock horns together like any deer in the herd.
Wilt thou ever be a foul-mouth'd and calumnious knave?
Will you always be a foul-mouthed, slandering rogue?
A prophet I, madam; and I speak the truth the next way: / For I the ballad will repeat, / Which men full true shall find; / Your marriage comes by destiny, / Your cuckoo sings by kind.
I'm a prophet, madam, and I speak the truth the quickest way: "For I the ballad will repeat, which men will find is true: your marriage comes by destiny, the cuckoo sings by nature."
Get you gone, sir; I'll talk with you more anon.
Go away, sir. I'll talk to you more later.
May it please you, madam, that he bid Helen come to you; of her I am to / speak.
If you please, madam, tell him to ask Helen to come to you. It's her I have to speak about.
Sirrah, tell my gentlewoman I would speak with her; Helen I mean.
Fellow, tell my young lady I want to speak to her. Helen, I mean.

[Sings] / Was this fair face the cause, quoth she, / Why the Grecians sacked Troy? / Fond done, done fond, / Was this King Priam's joy? / With that she sighed as she stood, / With that she sighed as she stood, / And gave this sentence then: / Among nine bad if one be good, / Among nine bad if one be good, / There's yet one good in ten.

[Sings] "Was this lovely face the reason," she said, "why the Greeks destroyed Troy? Foolishly done, done foolishly; was this King Priam's joy?" With that she sighed as she stood, and then gave this verdict: "Among nine bad, if one is good, there's still one good in ten."
What, one good in ten? You corrupt the song, sirrah.
What, one good in ten? You're spoiling the song, fellow.

One good woman in ten, madam, which is a purifying o' the song. Would / God would serve the world so all the year! We'd find no fault with the / tithe-woman, if I were the parson. One in ten, quoth 'a! And we might / have a good woman born but or every blazing star, or at an earthquake, / 'twould mend the lottery well; a man may draw his heart out ere he / pluck one.

One good woman in ten, madam: that's improving the song. I wish God would treat the world like that all year! We'd find no fault with the tenth woman if I were the parson. One in ten, he says! If only a good woman were born at every comet or every earthquake, it would improve the lottery a lot. As it is, a man could pull his heart out before he picked one.
You'll be gone, sir knave, and do as I command you!
Will you go, sir rogue, and do as I tell you!

That man should be at woman's command, and yet no hurt done! Though / honesty be no puritan, yet it will do no hurt; it will wear the / surplice of humility over the black gown of a big heart. I am going, / forsooth; the business is for Helen to come hither.

To think that a man should take orders from a woman and no harm be done! Though honesty is no Puritan, it will do no harm: it will wear the white robe of humility over the black gown of a proud heart. I'm going, indeed. The business is for Helen to come here.
I know, madam, you love your gentlewoman entirely.
I know, madam, that you love your young lady completely.

Faith I do. Her father bequeath'd her to me, and she herself, without / other advantage, may lawfully make title to as much love as she finds; / there is more owing her than is paid, and more shall be paid her than / she'll demand.
I certainly do. Her father left her to me, and she herself, with no other advantage, deserves all the love she gets. She is owed more than she's paid, and she'll be paid more than she asks for.

Madam, I was very late more near her than I think she wish'd me; alone / she was, and did communicate to herself her own words to her own ears; / she thought, I dare vow for her, they touch'd not any stranger sense. / Her matter was, she loved your son. Fortune, she said, was no goddess, / that had put such difference betwixt their two estates; Love no god, / that would not extend his might only where qualities were level; Diana / no queen of virgins, that would suffer her poor knight surpris'd, / without rescue in the first assault or ransom afterward. This she / deliver'd in the most bitter touch of sorrow that e'er I heard virgin / exclaim in, which I held my duty speedily to acquaint you withal; / sithence, in the loss that may happen, it concerns you something to / know it.

Madam, I was much nearer her just now than I think she wanted. She was alone, and speaking her own words to her own ears. She thought, I'd swear, that no one else could hear. What she said was that she loved your son. Fortune, she said, was no goddess, to have put such a difference between their two ranks; Love was no god, if he would only use his power where people were equal; Diana was no queen of virgins, if she let her poor follower be captured in the first attack with no rescue, or ransom afterwards. She said this in the most bitter sorrow I ever heard a young woman speak in. I thought it my duty to tell you quickly, since, in case anything bad comes of it, it is your concern to know.

You have discharg'd this honestly; keep it to yourself; many / likelihoods inform'd me of this before, which hung so tottering in the / balance that I could neither believe nor misdoubt. Pray you leave me; / stall this in your bosom; and I thank you for your honest care. I will / speak with you further anon.

You've done this honestly. Keep it to yourself. Many signs told me this before, but they hung so unsteadily in the balance that I could neither believe nor doubt it. Please leave me. Lock this away in your heart, and thank you for your honest care. I'll talk to you more later.

Even so it was with me when I was young; / If ever we are nature's, these are ours; this thorn / Doth to our rose of youth rightly belong; / Our blood to us, this to our blood is born; / It is the show and seal of nature's truth, / Where love's strong passion is impress'd in youth. / By our remembrances of days foregone, / Such were our faults, or then we thought them none. / Her eye is sick on't; I observe her now.

It was just like this with me when I was young. If we are nature's creatures at all, these feelings belong to us. This thorn rightly belongs to the rose of youth; our passions are born with us, and this is born with our passions. It is the mark and seal of nature's truth when love's strong passion is stamped on someone young. When we remember days gone by, we see these were our faults, or else we thought them none. Her eyes are sick with it; I can see it in her now.
You know, Helen, / I am a mother to you.
You know, Helen, I am a mother to you.

Nay, a mother. / Why not a mother? When I said a mother, / Methought you saw a serpent. What's in mother, / That you start at it? I say I am your mother, / And put you in the catalogue of those / That were enwombed mine. 'Tis often seen / Adoption strives with nature, and choice breeds / A native slip to us from foreign seeds. / You ne'er oppress'd me with a mother's groan, / Yet I express to you a mother's care. / God's mercy, maiden! does it curd thy blood / To say I am thy mother? What's the matter, / That this distempered messenger of wet, / The many-colour'd Iris, rounds thine eye? / —Why, that you are my daughter?

No, a mother. Why not a mother? When I said "mother", I thought you looked as if you'd seen a snake. What is there in "mother" that makes you start? I say I am your mother, and I put you on the list of those born from my womb. We often see adoption compete with nature, and choice grow a branch of our own from someone else's seed. You never made me groan in childbirth, yet I show you a mother's care. God's mercy, girl! Does it curdle your blood to hear me say I'm your mother? What's the matter, that this upset messenger of rain, the many-coloured rainbow, rings your eye? Why, because you're my daughter?
I say, I am your mother.
I say, I am your mother.

Pardon, madam; / The Count Rossillon cannot be my brother. / I am from humble, he from honoured name; / No note upon my parents, his all noble, / My master, my dear lord he is; and I / His servant live, and will his vassal die. / He must not be my brother.

Forgive me, madam. The Count of Rossillon can't be my brother. I come from a humble family, he from an honoured one. My parents are unknown; his are all noble. He's my master, my dear lord, and I live as his servant and will die as his subject. He must not be my brother.
And I can't be your mother?

You are my mother, madam; would you were— / So that my lord your son were not my brother,— / Indeed my mother! or were you both our mothers, / I care no more for than I do for heaven, / So I were not his sister. Can't no other, / But, I your daughter, he must be my brother?

You are my mother, madam. I wish you really were my mother, as long as my lord your son were not my brother! Or if you were mother to us both, I'd want that as much as I want heaven, as long as I weren't his sister. Is there no other way? If I'm your daughter, must he be my brother?

Yes, Helen, you might be my daughter-in-law. / God shield you mean it not! daughter and mother / So strive upon your pulse. What! pale again? / My fear hath catch'd your fondness; now I see / The mystery of your loneliness, and find / Your salt tears' head. Now to all sense 'tis gross / You love my son; invention is asham'd, / Against the proclamation of thy passion / To say thou dost not. Therefore tell me true; / But tell me then, 'tis so; for, look, thy cheeks / Confess it, t'one to th'other; and thine eyes / See it so grossly shown in thy behaviours, / That in their kind they speak it; only sin / And hellish obstinacy tie thy tongue, / That truth should be suspected. Speak, is't so? / If it be so, you have wound a goodly clew; / If it be not, forswear't: howe'er, I charge thee, / As heaven shall work in me for thine avail, / To tell me truly.

Yes, Helen, you could be my daughter-in-law. God forbid that's what you mean! "Daughter" and "mother" make your pulse race so. What, pale again? My fear has caught your love. Now I see the secret of your loneliness, and find the source of your salty tears. Now it's plain to anyone that you love my son. Excuses are ashamed to deny it against what your passion proclaims. So tell me the truth, and tell me it is so, because look, your cheeks confess it to each other, and your eyes see it so plainly in your behaviour that they speak it in their own way. Only sin and wicked stubbornness tie your tongue, so that the truth is doubted. Speak: is it so? If it is, you've wound yourself a fine tangle. If it isn't, swear it isn't. Either way, I order you, as heaven will help me to help you, to tell me truly.
Do not you love him, madam?
Go not about; my love hath in't a bond / Whereof the world takes note. Come, come, disclose / The state of your affection, for your passions / Have to the full appeach'd.
Don't go round the point. My love for him has a bond that the whole world knows about. Come, come, reveal what you feel, because your passions have fully given you away.

Then I confess, / Here on my knee, before high heaven and you, / That before you, and next unto high heaven, / I love your son. / My friends were poor, but honest; so's my love. / Be not offended; for it hurts not him / That he is lov'd of me; I follow him not / By any token of presumptuous suit, / Nor would I have him till I do deserve him; / Yet never know how that desert should be. / I know I love in vain, strive against hope; / Yet in this captious and inteemable sieve / I still pour in the waters of my love / And lack not to lose still. Thus, Indian-like, / Religious in mine error, I adore / The sun that looks upon his worshipper, / But knows of him no more. My dearest madam, / Let not your hate encounter with my love, / For loving where you do; but if yourself, / Whose aged honour cites a virtuous youth, / Did ever, in so true a flame of liking, / Wish chastely, and love dearly, that your Dian / Was both herself and love; O then, give pity / To her whose state is such that cannot choose / But lend and give where she is sure to lose; / That seeks not to find that her search implies, / But riddle-like, lives sweetly where she dies!

Then I confess, here on my knees, before high heaven and you, that more than you, and next only to high heaven, I love your son. My family were poor but honest, and so is my love. Don't be offended, because it does him no harm that I love him. I don't pursue him with any sign of presumptuous wooing, nor would I have him until I deserve him, and yet I don't know how I ever could. I know I love in vain and struggle against hope. Yet into this deceiving sieve that holds nothing I keep pouring the waters of my love, and never run short of more to lose. So, like a sun-worshipper in India, devoted in my mistake, I adore the sun, which looks down on its worshipper but knows nothing more of him. My dearest madam, don't let your hate meet my love because I love the one you love. If you yourself, whose honourable old age points to a virtuous youth, ever in so true a flame of love wished chastely and loved dearly, so that your Diana was both chaste and loving, then pity a woman whose situation means she can only lend and give where she's sure to lose; who doesn't try to find what she's searching for, but, like a riddle, lives sweetly where she dies!
Had you not lately an intent,—speak truly,— / To go to Paris?
Didn't you mean, not long ago (tell the truth), to go to Paris?

I will tell truth; by grace itself I swear. / You know my father left me some prescriptions / Of rare and prov'd effects, such as his reading / And manifest experience had collected / For general sovereignty; and that he will'd me / In heedfull'st reservation to bestow them, / As notes whose faculties inclusive were / More than they were in note. Amongst the rest / There is a remedy, approv'd, set down, / To cure the desperate languishings whereof / The king is render'd lost.

I'll tell the truth; I swear by grace itself. You know my father left me some prescriptions with rare and proven effects, which his reading and plain experience had collected as cures for everything, and that he told me to keep them with the greatest care, as notes whose powers were greater than people knew. Among them is a remedy, tested and written down, to cure the hopeless wasting illness that the King is said to be lost to.
This was your motive / For Paris, was it? Speak.
Was this your reason for going to Paris? Speak.
My lord your son made me to think of this; / Else Paris, and the medicine, and the king, / Had from the conversation of my thoughts / Haply been absent then.
My lord your son made me think of it. Otherwise Paris and the medicine and the King might never have crossed my mind.

But think you, Helen, / If you should tender your supposed aid, / He would receive it? He and his physicians / Are of a mind; he, that they cannot help him; / They, that they cannot help. How shall they credit / A poor unlearned virgin, when the schools, / Embowell'd of their doctrine, have let off / The danger to itself?

But do you think, Helen, if you offered your supposed help, he would accept it? He and his doctors agree: he, that they can't help him; they, that they can't help. How will they believe a poor, uneducated young woman, when the medical schools have emptied out all their learning and left the illness to run its course?

There's something in't / More than my father's skill, which was the great'st / Of his profession, that his good receipt / Shall for my legacy be sanctified / By th' luckiest stars in heaven; and would your honour / But give me leave to try success, I'd venture / The well-lost life of mine on his grace's cure. / By such a day, an hour.

There's something in it beyond my father's skill, though that was the greatest in his profession: I feel his good prescription will be blessed by the luckiest stars in heaven as my inheritance. If your honour would only let me try, I'd risk my life, which would be well lost, on curing his majesty by such and such a day and hour.

Why, Helen, thou shalt have my leave and love, / Means and attendants, and my loving greetings / To those of mine in court. I'll stay at home, / And pray God's blessing into thy attempt. / Be gone tomorrow; and be sure of this, / What I can help thee to, thou shalt not miss.

Why, Helen, you shall have my permission and my love, money and servants, and my loving greetings to my friends at court. I'll stay at home and pray for God's blessing on your attempt. Leave tomorrow, and be sure of this: whatever I can help you with, you won't go without.

Farewell, young lords; these warlike principles / Do not throw from you; and you, my lords, farewell; / Share the advice betwixt you; if both gain all, / The gift doth stretch itself as 'tis receiv'd, / And is enough for both.

Goodbye, young lords. Don't throw away these principles of war. And you, my lords, goodbye too. Share the advice between you. If each of you takes all of it, the gift stretches as it's received, and there's enough for both.
'Tis our hope, sir, / After well-ent'red soldiers, to return / And find your grace in health.
We hope, sir, after we've seasoned ourselves as soldiers, to come back and find your grace in good health.

No, no, it cannot be; and yet my heart / Will not confess he owes the malady / That doth my life besiege. Farewell, young lords. / Whether I live or die, be you the sons / Of worthy Frenchmen; let higher Italy,— / Those bated that inherit but the fall / Of the last monarchy—see that you come / Not to woo honour, but to wed it, when / The bravest questant shrinks: find what you seek, / That fame may cry you loud. I say farewell.

No, no, that can't be. And yet my heart won't admit it suffers from the illness that is besieging my life. Goodbye, young lords. Whether I live or die, show yourselves the sons of worthy Frenchmen. Let northern Italy (except those who have inherited only the fall of the last empire) see that you come not to court honour but to marry it. Where the bravest seeker shrinks back, find what you are looking for, so that fame shouts your name aloud. I say goodbye.
Health, at your bidding serve your majesty!
May health obey your command and serve your majesty!
Those girls of Italy, take heed of them; / They say our French lack language to deny / If they demand; beware of being captives / Before you serve.
Those Italian girls: watch out for them. They say we French have no words to say no if they ask. Be careful not to be taken prisoner before you've even fought.
Our hearts take in your warnings.
O my sweet lord, that you will stay behind us!
Oh, my dear lord, to think you're staying behind!
It's not his fault, the young spark.
Most admirable! I have seen those wars.
Wonderful! I have seen those wars.
I am commanded here, and kept a coil with, / "Too young", and "the next year" and "'tis too early".
I'm ordered to stay here, and pestered with "too young" and "next year" and "it's too early".
An thy mind stand to't, boy, steal away bravely.
If your heart is set on it, boy, slip away bravely.
I shall stay here the forehorse to a smock, / Creaking my shoes on the plain masonry, / Till honour be bought up, and no sword worn / But one to dance with. By heaven, I'll steal away.

I'll stay here leading a woman's skirt like the front horse of a team, squeaking my shoes on the smooth floors, until all the honour is used up and nobody wears a sword except to dance with. By heaven, I'll slip away.
I am your accessary; and so farewell.
I'm your accomplice. And so, goodbye.
I grow to you, and our parting is a tortur'd body.
I've grown into you, and parting from you is like tearing a body apart.

Noble heroes, my sword and yours are kin. Good sparks and lustrous, a / word, good metals. You shall find in the regiment of the Spinii one / Captain Spurio, with his cicatrice, an emblem of war, here on his / sinister cheek; it was this very sword entrench'd it. Say to him I / live; and observe his reports for me.

Noble heroes, my sword and yours are related. Good, shining sparks, a word, my fine metals. In the Spinii regiment you'll find a Captain Spurio, with a scar, a badge of war, here on his left cheek. It was this very sword that carved it. Tell him I'm alive, and note what he says about me.
Mars dote on you for his novices!
May Mars love you as his apprentices!

Use a more spacious ceremony to the noble lords; you have restrain'd / yourself within the list of too cold an adieu. Be more expressive to / them; for they wear themselves in the cap of the time; there do muster / true gait; eat, speak, and move, under the influence of the most / receiv'd star; and though the devil lead the measure, such are to be / followed. After them, and take a more dilated farewell.

Give the noble lords a more generous goodbye. You kept yourself within the limits of too cold a farewell. Be more open with them, because they're the jewel in the cap of fashion. They show off the right way to walk, they eat, speak and move under the most fashionable star, and even if the devil leads the dance, men like that should be followed. Go after them, and say a fuller goodbye.
Worthy fellows, and like to prove most sinewy sword-men.
Fine fellows, and likely to turn out very strong swordsmen.
Pardon, my lord [Kneeling], for me and for my tidings.
Forgive me, my lord, [Kneeling] for myself and for my news.
I'll fee thee to stand up.
I'll pay you to stand up.
Then here's a man stands that has brought his pardon. / I would you had kneel'd, my lord, to ask me mercy, / And that at my bidding you could so stand up.
Then here's a man who has bought his pardon standing. I wish, my lord, that you had knelt to ask me for mercy, and that you could stand up when I told you to.
I would I had; so I had broke thy pate, / And ask'd thee mercy for't.
I wish I had: then I'd have broken your head and asked you to forgive me for it.
Good faith, across; / But, my good lord, 'tis thus: will you be cur'd / Of your infirmity?
Well, that's a miss. But, my good lord, it's like this: do you want to be cured of your illness?

O, will you eat / No grapes, my royal fox? Yes, but you will / My noble grapes, and if my royal fox / Could reach them. I have seen a medicine / That's able to breathe life into a stone, / Quicken a rock, and make you dance canary / With sprightly fire and motion; whose simple touch / Is powerful to araise King Pippen, nay, / To give great Charlemain a pen in's hand / And write to her a love-line.

Oh, won't you eat any grapes, my royal fox? Yes, you would eat my noble grapes, if my royal fox could reach them. I have seen a medicine that can breathe life into a stone, bring a rock to life, and make you dance a lively canary dance with fiery energy. Its mere touch has the power to raise King Pepin from the dead, or even to put a pen in great Charlemagne's hand and have him write her a love poem.

Why, doctor 'she'! My lord, there's one arriv'd, / If you will see her. Now, by my faith and honour, / If seriously I may convey my thoughts / In this my light deliverance, I have spoke / With one that in her sex, her years, profession, / Wisdom, and constancy, hath amaz'd me more / Than I dare blame my weakness. Will you see her, / For that is her demand, and know her business? / That done, laugh well at me.

Why, a lady doctor! My lord, someone has arrived, if you'll see her. Now, on my faith and honour, if I can say something serious in this light way of talking, I have spoken with a woman who, for her sex, her age, her profession, her wisdom and her steadiness, has amazed me more than I can blame on my own weakness. Will you see her (that's what she asks) and hear her business? Once that's done, laugh at me all you like.
Now, good Lafew, / Bring in the admiration; that we with thee / May spend our wonder too, or take off thine / By wond'ring how thou took'st it.
Now, good Lafew, bring in this wonder, so that we can share your amazement, or cure you of yours by wondering how you caught it.
Nay, I'll fit you, / And not be all day neither.
No, I'll prove it to you, and not take all day about it either.
Thus he his special nothing ever prologues.
He always makes a grand introduction to his special nothings.
This haste really does have wings.

Nay, come your ways. / This is his majesty, say your mind to him. / A traitor you do look like, but such traitors / His majesty seldom fears; I am Cressid's uncle, / That dare leave two together. Fare you well.

Come along. This is his majesty: tell him what you have in mind. You look like a traitor, but his majesty rarely fears traitors like you. I'm like Cressida's uncle, who dared to leave two people alone together. Goodbye.
Now, fair one, does your business follow us?
Now, beautiful lady, does your business concern us?
Ay, my good lord. / Gerard de Narbon was my father, / In what he did profess, well found.
Yes, my good lord. Gerard de Narbon was my father, and he was highly skilled in his profession.

The rather will I spare my praises towards him. / Knowing him is enough. On his bed of death / Many receipts he gave me; chiefly one, / Which, as the dearest issue of his practice, / And of his old experience the only darling, / He bade me store up as a triple eye, / Safer than mine own two; more dear I have so, / And hearing your high majesty is touch'd / With that malignant cause, wherein the honour / Of my dear father's gift stands chief in power, / I come to tender it, and my appliance, / With all bound humbleness.

Then I'll spare my praise of him; knowing him is enough. On his deathbed he gave me many prescriptions, and one above all, the dearest result of his practice and the only darling of his long experience. He told me to treasure it like a third eye, more safely than my own two. I have done so. And hearing that your majesty is afflicted with the very illness in which my dear father's gift is most powerful, I've come to offer it, and my treatment, in all due humility.

We thank you, maiden, / But may not be so credulous of cure, / When our most learned doctors leave us, and / The congregated college have concluded / That labouring art can never ransom nature / From her inaidable estate. I say we must not / So stain our judgment, or corrupt our hope, / To prostitute our past-cure malady / To empirics, or to dissever so / Our great self and our credit, to esteem / A senseless help, when help past sense we deem.

We thank you, young lady, but we can't be so ready to believe in a cure, when our most learned doctors have given up on us, and the whole college of physicians has concluded that their hard-working skill can never rescue nature from her hopeless state. I say we must not so stain our judgement, or spoil our hope, as to hand over our incurable illness to quacks, or so split our royal self from our reputation as to value a senseless remedy when we think we're past all sensible help.
My duty then shall pay me for my pains. / I will no more enforce mine office on you, / Humbly entreating from your royal thoughts / A modest one to bear me back again.
Then my sense of duty will be my reward for my trouble. I won't force my services on you any more. I humbly ask your royal mind for one modest thought to take back home with me.

I cannot give thee less, to be call'd grateful. / Thou thought'st to help me; and such thanks I give / As one near death to those that wish him live. / But what at full I know, thou know'st no part; / I knowing all my peril, thou no art.

I can't give you less if I want to be called grateful. You meant to help me, and I give you the kind of thanks a dying man gives to those who wish him to live. But what I fully know, you don't know at all: I know all my danger, and you know no cure for it.

What I can do can do no hurt to try, / Since you set up your rest 'gainst remedy. / He that of greatest works is finisher / Oft does them by the weakest minister. / So holy writ in babes hath judgment shown, / When judges have been babes. Great floods have flown / From simple sources, and great seas have dried / When miracles have by the great'st been denied. / Oft expectation fails, and most oft there / Where most it promises; and oft it hits / Where hope is coldest, and despair most fits.

There's no harm in trying what I can do, since you've staked everything against any remedy. God, who finishes the greatest works, often does them through the weakest servant. So the Bible shows wisdom in babies when judges have behaved like babies. Great floods have flowed from small springs, and great seas have dried up when the greatest men refused to believe in miracles. Expectation often fails, and most often where it promises most; and it often succeeds where hope is coldest and despair seems most fitting.
I must not hear thee. Fare thee well, kind maid. / Thy pains, not us'd, must by thyself be paid; / Proffers, not took, reap thanks for their reward.
I mustn't listen to you. Goodbye, kind girl. Since your efforts aren't used, you must pay yourself for them. Offers that are not accepted earn thanks as their reward.

Inspired merit so by breath is barr'd. / It is not so with Him that all things knows / As 'tis with us that square our guess by shows; / But most it is presumption in us when / The help of heaven we count the act of men. / Dear sir, to my endeavours give consent; / Of heaven, not me, make an experiment. / I am not an impostor, that proclaim / Myself against the level of mine aim, / But know I think, and think I know most sure, / My art is not past power nor you past cure.

So inspired worth is shut out by a word. It isn't like this with God, who knows everything, as it is with us, who judge by appearances. But it is the greatest presumption in us when we count heaven's help as the work of human beings. Dear sir, agree to my attempt. Make a trial of heaven, not of me. I'm not a fraud who claims more than I can hit. Know that I think, and think I know for certain, that my skill is not powerless and you are not past cure.
Art thou so confident? Within what space / Hop'st thou my cure?
Are you so confident? How soon do you hope to cure me?

The greatest grace lending grace. / Ere twice the horses of the sun shall bring / Their fiery torcher his diurnal ring, / Ere twice in murk and occidental damp / Moist Hesperus hath quench'd her sleepy lamp; / Or four and twenty times the pilot's glass / Hath told the thievish minutes how they pass; / What is infirm from your sound parts shall fly, / Health shall live free, and sickness freely die.

With God's grace helping, before the horses of the sun have twice carried their fiery torch round its daily circle; before the evening star has twice put out her sleepy lamp in the dark western mist; or before the sailor's hourglass has counted the stealing minutes twenty-four times, whatever is sick will leave your healthy parts. Health will live free, and sickness will die.
Upon thy certainty and confidence / What dar'st thou venture?
If you're so sure and confident, what do you dare to risk?

Tax of impudence, / A strumpet's boldness, a divulged shame, / Traduc'd by odious ballads; my maiden's name / Sear'd otherwise; nay worse of worst extended / With vilest torture, let my life be ended.

Being charged with shamelessness, with a whore's boldness; a public disgrace, mocked in vile ballads; my good name as a virgin branded; or worse than the worst, let my life be ended with the cruellest torture.

Methinks in thee some blessed spirit doth speak / His powerful sound within an organ weak; / And what impossibility would slay / In common sense, sense saves another way. / Thy life is dear, for all that life can rate / Worth name of life in thee hath estimate: / Youth, beauty, wisdom, courage, all / That happiness and prime can happy call. / Thou this to hazard needs must intimate / Skill infinite, or monstrous desperate. / Sweet practiser, thy physic I will try, / That ministers thine own death if I die.

I think some blessed spirit speaks its powerful voice through you, a weak instrument. What common sense would rule impossible, a higher sense saves another way. Your life is precious, because everything that makes life worth the name is valued in you: youth, beauty, wisdom, courage, everything that happiness and the prime of life can call happy. To risk all this, you must have either infinite skill or monstrous desperation. Sweet doctor, I will try your medicine, which will bring about your own death if I die.
If I break time, or flinch in property / Of what I spoke, unpitied let me die, / And well deserv'd. Not helping, death's my fee; / But if I help, what do you promise me?
If I miss the time, or fail in any detail of what I've said, let me die unpitied, and deservedly. If I don't help, death is my payment. But if I do help, what do you promise me?
But will you make it even?
Ay, by my sceptre and my hopes of heaven.
Yes, by my sceptre and my hopes of heaven.

Then shalt thou give me, with thy kingly hand / What husband in thy power I will command: / Exempted be from me the arrogance / To choose from forth the royal blood of France, / My low and humble name to propagate / With any branch or image of thy state; / But such a one, thy vassal, whom I know / Is free for me to ask, thee to bestow.

Then you will give me, with your royal hand, whatever husband in your power I ask for. I won't be so arrogant as to choose from the royal blood of France, to join my low and humble name with any branch or image of your royal line; but one of your subjects whom I know I'm free to ask for and you're free to give.

Here is my hand; the premises observ'd, / Thy will by my performance shall be serv'd; / So make the choice of thy own time, for I, / Thy resolv'd patient, on thee still rely. / More should I question thee, and more I must, / Though more to know could not be more to trust: / From whence thou cam'st, how tended on; but rest / Unquestion'd welcome, and undoubted bless'd. / Give me some help here, ho! If thou proceed / As high as word, my deed shall match thy deed.

Here is my hand. If you keep to your terms, I'll keep my promise and do your will. So choose your own time, because I, your determined patient, rely on you completely. I ought to question you more, and I must, though knowing more could not make me trust you more: where you come from, who came with you. But stay unquestioned and welcome, and blessed beyond doubt. Help me here, someone! If you do as much as you've said, my actions will match yours.
Come on, sir; I shall now put you to the height of your breeding.
Come on, sir. Now I'll put your upbringing to the highest test.
I will show myself highly fed and lowly taught. I know my business is / but to the court.
I'll show myself well fed and badly taught. I know my business is only to go to court.
To the court! Why, what place make you special, when you put off that / with such contempt? But to the court!
Only to court! Why, what place do you think so special, when you dismiss the court with such contempt? "Only to court"!

Truly, madam, if God have lent a man any manners, he may easily put it / off at court: he that cannot make a leg, put off's cap, kiss his hand, / and say nothing, has neither leg, hands, lip, nor cap; and indeed such / a fellow, to say precisely, were not for the court; but for me, I have / an answer will serve all men.

Honestly, madam, if God has lent a man any manners, he can easily show them off at court. Anyone who can't bow, take off his cap, kiss his hand and say nothing has no leg, no hands, no lips and no cap, and to be precise, such a fellow isn't fit for court. But as for me, I have an answer that will do for everyone.
Marry, that's a bountiful answer that fits all questions.
Well, that's a generous answer if it fits every question.
It is like a barber's chair, that fits all buttocks—the pin-buttock, / the quatch-buttock, the brawn-buttock, or any buttock.
It's like a barber's chair, which fits every backside: the thin backside, the squat backside, the fat backside, any backside.
Will your answer serve fit to all questions?
Will your answer really fit every question?

As fit as ten groats is for the hand of an attorney, as your French / crown for your taffety punk, as Tib's rush for Tom's forefinger, as a / pancake for Shrove-Tuesday, a morris for May-day, as the nail to his / hole, the cuckold to his horn, as a scolding quean to a wrangling / knave, as the nun's lip to the friar's mouth; nay, as the pudding to / his skin.

As well as ten groats fit a lawyer's hand, a French crown fits a dressed-up whore, Tib's rush ring fits Tom's finger, a pancake fits Shrove Tuesday, a morris dance fits May Day, a nail fits its hole, a cuckold fits his horns, a nagging woman fits a quarrelling rogue, the nun's lip fits the friar's mouth; yes, as the sausage fits its skin.
Have you, I say, an answer of such fitness for all questions?
I ask you again, do you have an answer that fits all questions so well?
From below your duke to beneath your constable, it will fit any / question.
From your duke down to below your constable, it'll fit any question.
It must be an answer of most monstrous size that must fit all demands.
It must be an answer of enormous size if it fits every question.
But a trifle neither, in good faith, if the learned should speak truth / of it. Here it is, and all that belongs to't. Ask me if I am a / courtier; it shall do you no harm to learn.
It's only a trifle, honestly, if the learned told the truth about it. Here it is, and everything that goes with it. Ask me if I'm a courtier. It won't do you any harm to learn.
To be young again, if we could: I will be a fool in question, hoping to / be the wiser by your answer. I pray you, sir, are you a courtier?
To be young again, if only we could! I'll play the fool by asking, hoping to be wiser for your answer. Tell me, sir, are you a courtier?
O Lord, sir! There's a simple putting off. More, more, a hundred of / them.
"O Lord, sir!" There's an easy way to dodge a question. More, more, a hundred of them.
Sir, I am a poor friend of yours, that loves you.
Sir, I'm a poor friend of yours who loves you.
O Lord, sir! Thick, thick; spare not me.
"O Lord, sir!" Quick, quick, don't spare me.
I think, sir, you can eat none of this homely meat.
I don't suppose, sir, you can eat any of this plain food.
O Lord, sir! Nay, put me to't, I warrant you.
"O Lord, sir!" Go on, test me, I promise you.
You were lately whipp'd, sir, as I think.
I think you were whipped recently, sir.
O Lord, sir! Spare not me.
Do you cry 'O Lord, sir!' at your whipping, and 'spare not me'? Indeed / your 'O Lord, sir!' is very sequent to your whipping. You would answer / very well to a whipping, if you were but bound to't.

Do you cry "O Lord, sir!" and "Don't spare me" when you're whipped? Indeed your "O Lord, sir!" follows very naturally from a whipping. You'd make a very good answer to a whipping, if only you were tied up for it.
I ne'er had worse luck in my life in my 'O Lord, sir!' I see things may / serve long, but not serve ever.
I've never had worse luck in my life with my "O Lord, sir!" I see things can be useful for a long time, but not for ever.
I play the noble housewife with the time, to entertain it so merrily / with a fool.
I'm being a fine housewife with my time, spending it so merrily with a fool.
O Lord, sir! Why, there't serves well again.
"O Lord, sir!" Why, there it works again.
An end, sir! To your business. Give Helen this, / And urge her to a present answer back. / Commend me to my kinsmen and my son. / This is not much.
Enough, sir! Get on with your business. Give Helen this, and urge her to send an answer back at once. Give my regards to my relatives and my son. This isn't much.
Not much of a greeting to them?
Not much employment for you. You understand me?
Not much work for you. Do you understand me?
Most fruitfully. I am there before my legs.
Very well. I'll be there before my legs.

They say miracles are past; and we have our philosophical persons to / make modern and familiar things supernatural and causeless. Hence is it / that we make trifles of terrors, ensconcing ourselves into seeming / knowledge when we should submit ourselves to an unknown fear.

They say the age of miracles is over, and we have our philosophers who make supernatural things seem ordinary and explainable. That's why we make light of terrible things, hiding behind a show of knowledge when we should give in to a fear of the unknown.
Why, 'tis the rarest argument of wonder that hath shot out in our / latter times.
Why, it's the most extraordinary wonder to appear in recent times.
To be relinquish'd of the artists,—
To be given up by the experts...
So I say; both of Galen and Paracelsus.
That's what I say: by followers of both Galen and Paracelsus.
Of all the learned and authentic fellows,—
By all the learned and qualified men...
Why, there 'tis; so say I too.
Why, there it is. That's what I say too.
Right; as 'twere a man assur'd of a—
Right, like a man certain of a...
An uncertain life and a sure death.
Just; you say well. So would I have said.
Exactly, well said. That's what I would have said.
I may truly say, it is a novelty to the world.
I can truly say it's something new to the world.
It is indeed; if you will have it in showing, you shall read it in what / do you call there?
It is indeed. If you want it set out, you can read it in that, what do you call it?
A showing of a heavenly effect in an earthly actor.
"A demonstration of heavenly power in an earthly agent."
That's it; I would have said the very same.
That's it. I would have said exactly the same.
Why, your dolphin is not lustier; fore me, I speak in respect—
Why, a young dolphin isn't livelier than the King. Upon my soul, I say it with respect...
Nay, 'tis strange, 'tis very strange; that is the brief and the tedious / of it; and he's of a most facinerious spirit that will not acknowledge / it to be the—
No, it's strange, very strange, that's the long and short of it; and anyone who won't admit it is the... must have a very wicked spirit...
And debile minister, great power, great transcendence, which should / indeed give us a further use to be made than alone the recov'ry of the / king, as to be—
And feeble agent, great power, great transcendence, which should indeed be put to further use than just the King's recovery, so as to be...
I would have said it; you say well. Here comes the king.
I would have said that; you put it well. Here comes the King.
Lustique, as the Dutchman says. I'll like a maid the better, whilst I / have a tooth in my head. Why, he's able to lead her a coranto.
Lusty, as the Dutchman says! I'll like girls all the better while I have a tooth left in my head. Why, he's fit to lead her in a lively dance.
Mor du vinager! is not this Helen?
God's death and vinegar! Isn't that Helen?
Go, call before me all the lords in court.
Go and call all the lords at court to come before me.

Sit, my preserver, by thy patient's side, / And with this healthful hand, whose banish'd sense / Thou has repeal'd, a second time receive / The confirmation of my promis'd gift, / Which but attends thy naming.

Sit beside your patient, my saviour. With this healthy hand, whose lost feeling you have brought back, receive a second time the confirmation of the gift I promised you, which is only waiting for you to name it.

Fair maid, send forth thine eye. This youthful parcel / Of noble bachelors stand at my bestowing, / O'er whom both sovereign power and father's voice / I have to use. Thy frank election make; / Thou hast power to choose, and they none to forsake.

Beautiful girl, look around. This group of young noble bachelors is mine to give away, and over them I have both a king's power and a father's say. Make your choice freely: you have the power to choose, and they have none to refuse.
To each of you one fair and virtuous mistress / Fall, when love please! Marry, to each but one!
May each of you find a beautiful and virtuous wife, whenever Love pleases! Well, one each, at least!
I'd give bay curtal and his furniture / My mouth no more were broken than these boys', / And writ as little beard.
I'd give my bay horse with the docked tail, and all his harness, if my teeth were as unbroken as these boys' and I had as little beard.
Peruse them well. / Not one of those but had a noble father.
Look them over well. Every one of them had a noble father.
Gentlemen, / Heaven hath through me restor'd the king to health.
Gentlemen, heaven has restored the King to health through me.
We understand it, and thank heaven for you.
We know it, and thank heaven for you.

I am a simple maid, and therein wealthiest / That I protest I simply am a maid. / Please it, your majesty, I have done already. / The blushes in my cheeks thus whisper me: / "We blush that thou shouldst choose; but, be refused, / Let the white death sit on thy cheek for ever, / We'll ne'er come there again."

I'm a simple girl, and my greatest wealth is that I can say I'm simply a virgin. If it please your majesty, I've finished already. The blushes in my cheeks whisper to me: "We blush that you should choose; but if you're refused, let pale death sit on your cheek for ever. We'll never come there again."
Make choice; and, see, / Who shuns thy love shuns all his love in me.
Make your choice. And mark this: anyone who rejects your love rejects all my love for him.
Now, Dian, from thy altar do I fly, / And to imperial Love, that god most high, / Do my sighs stream. [To first Lord] Sir, will you hear my suit?
Now, Diana, I run from your altar, and to imperial Love, that highest god, my sighs flow. [To first Lord] Sir, will you hear my request?
Thanks, sir; all the rest is mute.
Thank you, sir. All the rest is silence.
I had rather be in this choice than throw ames-ace for my life.
I'd rather be in this lottery than throw a double one at dice with my life at stake.
[To second Lord] The honour, sir, that flames in your fair eyes, / Before I speak, too threat'ningly replies. / Love make your fortunes twenty times above / Her that so wishes, and her humble love!

[To second Lord] The pride, sir, that burns in your fine eyes answers me too threateningly before I even speak. May Love make your fortune twenty times higher than she who wishes it, and her humble love!
No better than that, if you please.
My wish receive, / Which great Love grant; and so I take my leave.
Take my wish, which may great Love grant; and so I take my leave.
Do all they deny her? An they were sons of mine I'd have them whipp'd; / or I would send them to th' Turk to make eunuchs of.
Are they all refusing her? If they were my sons, I'd have them whipped, or send them to the Turks to be made eunuchs.
[To third Lord] Be not afraid that I your hand should take; / I'll never do you wrong for your own sake. / Blessing upon your vows, and in your bed / Find fairer fortune, if you ever wed!
[To third Lord] Don't be afraid I'll take your hand. I'd never wrong you, for your own sake. Bless your vows, and may you find better fortune in your bed, if you ever marry!
These boys are boys of ice, they'll none have her. Sure, they are / bastards to the English; the French ne'er got 'em.
These boys are boys of ice; none of them will have her. They must be English bastards; no Frenchman ever fathered them.
[To fourth Lord] You are too young, too happy, and too good, / To make yourself a son out of my blood.
[To fourth Lord] You're too young, too lucky and too good to make yourself a son out of my blood.
Fair one, I think not so.
Beautiful lady, I don't think so.
There's one grape yet. I am sure thy father drank wine. But if thou / beest not an ass, I am a youth of fourteen; I have known thee already.
There's one good grape left. I'm sure your father drank wine. But if you're not an ass, I'm a fourteen-year-old boy. I've seen through you already.
[To Bertram] I dare not say I take you, but I give / Me and my service, ever whilst I live, / Into your guiding power. This is the man.
[To Bertram] I don't dare say I take you, but I give myself and my service, for as long as I live, into your guiding power. This is the man.
Why, then, young Bertram, take her; she's thy wife.
Why, then, young Bertram, take her. She's your wife.
My wife, my liege! I shall beseech your highness, / In such a business give me leave to use / The help of mine own eyes.
My wife, my lord! I beg your highness to let me use my own eyes in a matter like this.
Know'st thou not, Bertram, / What she has done for me?
Don't you know, Bertram, what she has done for me?
Yes, my good lord, / But never hope to know why I should marry her.
Yes, my good lord, but I never expect to know why I should marry her.
Thou know'st she has rais'd me from my sickly bed.
You know she has raised me from my sickbed.

But follows it, my lord, to bring me down / Must answer for your raising? I know her well; / She had her breeding at my father's charge: / A poor physician's daughter my wife! Disdain / Rather corrupt me ever!

But does it follow, my lord, that I must be brought down to pay for your raising? I know her well: she was brought up at my father's expense. A poor doctor's daughter my wife! I'd rather contempt ruined me for ever!

'Tis only title thou disdain'st in her, the which / I can build up.
