Strange is it that our bloods, / Of colour, weight, and heat, pour'd all together, / Would quite confound distinction, yet stands off / In differences so mighty. If she be / All that is virtuous, save what thou dislik'st, / A poor physician's daughter,—thou dislik'st— / Of virtue for the name. But do not so. / From lowest place when virtuous things proceed, / The place is dignified by the doer's deed. / Where great additions swell's, and virtue none, / It is a dropsied honour. Good alone / Is good without a name; vileness is so: / The property by what it is should go, / Not by the title. She is young, wise, fair; / In these to nature she's immediate heir; / And these breed honour: that is honour's scorn / Which challenges itself as honour's born, / And is not like the sire. Honours thrive / When rather from our acts we them derive / Than our fore-goers. The mere word's a slave, / Debauch'd on every tomb, on every grave / A lying trophy, and as oft is dumb / Where dust and damn'd oblivion is the tomb / Of honour'd bones indeed. What should be said? / If thou canst like this creature as a maid, / I can create the rest. Virtue and she / Is her own dower; honour and wealth from me.

It's only her rank you despise in her, and that I can build up. It's strange that our bloods, which if you poured them all together would be impossible to tell apart in colour, weight and heat, should stand apart with such great differences. If she is everything virtuous, except for what you dislike (a poor doctor's daughter), you dislike virtue because of a name. But don't do that. When virtuous deeds come from the lowest place, the place is honoured by the doer's deed. Where great titles puff someone up and there's no virtue, it is a swollen, diseased honour. Good is good on its own, without a name; so is wickedness. A thing should be judged by what it is, not by what it is called. She is young, wise and beautiful; she inherits these directly from nature, and these produce honour. The honour that claims to be honour's child but is not like its father deserves scorn. Honours flourish when we earn them by our own deeds rather than from our ancestors. The mere word is a slave, abused on every tomb, a lying trophy on every grave, and is just as often silent where dust and cursed forgetting are the only tomb of truly honourable bones. What more is there to say? If you can like this creature as a young woman, I can create the rest. Her virtue and herself are her own dowry; honour and wealth will come from me.
I cannot love her, nor will strive to do 't.
I can't love her, and I won't try to.
Thou wrong'st thyself, if thou shouldst strive to choose.
You wrong yourself if you try to choose for yourself.
That you are well restor'd, my lord, I am glad. / Let the rest go.
I'm glad, my lord, that you are well again. Let the rest go.

My honour's at the stake, which to defeat, / I must produce my power. Here, take her hand, / Proud scornful boy, unworthy this good gift, / That dost in vile misprision shackle up / My love and her desert; that canst not dream / We, poising us in her defective scale, / Shall weigh thee to the beam; that wilt not know / It is in us to plant thine honour where / We please to have it grow. Check thy contempt; / Obey our will, which travails in thy good; / Believe not thy disdain, but presently / Do thine own fortunes that obedient right / Which both thy duty owes and our power claims; / Or I will throw thee from my care for ever / Into the staggers and the careless lapse / Of youth and ignorance; both my revenge and hate / Loosing upon thee in the name of justice, / Without all terms of pity. Speak! Thine answer!

My honour is at stake, and to defend it I must use my power. Here, take her hand, you proud, scornful boy, unworthy of this good gift, who with your vile contempt chain up my love and her worth; who can't imagine that I, adding my weight to her lighter side of the scales, can outweigh you completely; who won't recognise that I have the power to plant your honour wherever I please. Hold back your contempt. Obey my will, which works for your good. Don't trust your disdain, but at once give your own fortunes the obedience that your duty owes and my power demands, or I'll throw you out of my care for ever into the staggering and reckless fall of youth and ignorance, letting loose both my revenge and my hatred on you in the name of justice, without any pity. Speak! Your answer!

Pardon, my gracious lord; for I submit / My fancy to your eyes. When I consider / What great creation, and what dole of honour / Flies where you bid it, I find that she, which late / Was in my nobler thoughts most base, is now / The praised of the king; who, so ennobled, / Is as 'twere born so.

Forgive me, my gracious lord, for I submit my likings to your eyes. When I consider what great promotions and what shares of honour go wherever you command, I find that she, who until now was the lowest in my noble thoughts, is now the one the King praises; and, so ennobled, she is as good as born noble.
Take her by the hand, / And tell her she is thine; to whom I promise / A counterpoise; if not to thy estate, / A balance more replete.
Take her by the hand and tell her she is yours. And I promise her a fortune to match yours, or, if not to match it, one that outweighs it.

Good fortune and the favour of the king / Smile upon this contract; whose ceremony / Shall seem expedient on the now-born brief, / And be perform'd tonight. The solemn feast / Shall more attend upon the coming space, / Expecting absent friends. As thou lov'st her, / Thy love's to me religious; else, does err.

May good fortune and the King's favour smile on this contract. Its ceremony shall follow quickly on this new agreement and be performed tonight. The formal wedding feast will wait a little longer, for absent friends to arrive. If you love her, your love to me is sacred; otherwise it is wrong.
Do you hear, monsieur? A word with you.
Listen, monsieur. A word with you.
Your lord and master did well to make his recantation.
Your lord and master did well to take back what he said.
Take it back! My lord! My master!
Ay. Is it not a language I speak?
Yes. Am I not speaking a language?
A most harsh one, and not to be understood without bloody succeeding. / My master!
A very harsh one, and not to be understood without bloodshed to follow. My master!
Are you companion to the Count Rossillon?
Are you the Count of Rossillon's companion?
To any count; to all counts; to what is man.
To any count; to all counts; to any man.
To what is count's man: count's master is of another style.
To any count's man: a count's master is called something else.
You are too old, sir; let it satisfy you, you are too old.
You're too old, sir. Let that be enough for you: you're too old.
I must tell thee, sirrah, I write man; to which title age cannot bring / thee.
I must tell you, fellow, I count myself a man, a title that age can't bring you to.
What I dare too well do, I dare not do.
What I dare do only too well, I don't dare do.

I did think thee, for two ordinaries, to be a pretty wise fellow; thou / didst make tolerable vent of thy travel; it might pass. Yet the scarfs / and the bannerets about thee did manifoldly dissuade me from believing / thee a vessel of too great a burden. I have now found thee; when I lose / thee again I care not. Yet art thou good for nothing but taking up, and / that thou art scarce worth.

For two dinners, I thought you were a reasonably wise fellow. You gave a tolerable account of your travels; it might pass. Yet the scarves and the ribbons all over you strongly put me off believing you were a ship with much cargo. Now I've found you out, and when I lose you again I won't care. You're good for nothing except being picked up, and you're hardly worth that.
Hadst thou not the privilege of antiquity upon thee—
If you didn't have the privilege of old age...

Do not plunge thyself too far in anger, lest thou hasten thy trial; / which if—Lord have mercy on thee for a hen! So, my good window of / lattice, fare thee well; thy casement I need not open, for I look / through thee. Give me thy hand.

Don't throw yourself too far into anger, or you'll bring on your own trial, and if... Lord have mercy on you for a chicken! So, my good lattice window, goodbye. I don't need to open your shutters; I can see straight through you. Give me your hand.
My lord, you give me most egregious indignity.
My lord, you insult me most outrageously.
Ay, with all my heart; and thou art worthy of it.
Yes, with all my heart, and you deserve it.
I have not, my lord, deserv'd it.
I haven't deserved it, my lord.
Yes, good faith, every dram of it; and I will not bate thee a scruple.
Yes, I swear, every drop of it, and I won't let you off a grain.

Ev'n as soon as thou canst, for thou hast to pull at a smack o' th' / contrary. If ever thou beest bound in thy scarf and beaten, thou shalt / find what it is to be proud of thy bondage. I have a desire to hold my / acquaintance with thee, or rather my knowledge, that I may say in the / default, "He is a man I know."

The sooner the better, because you've a lot of the opposite to drink up first. If you're ever tied up in your scarf and beaten, you'll find out what it means to be proud of your chains. I want to keep up my acquaintance with you, or rather my knowledge of you, so that when you fail I can say, "He is a man I know."
My lord, you do me most insupportable vexation.
My lord, you annoy me unbearably.
I would it were hell-pains for thy sake, and my poor doing eternal; for / doing I am past, as I will by thee, in what motion age will give me / leave.
I wish it were the pains of hell for your sake, and my poor efforts went on for ever. But I'm past doing, as I'll be past you, as fast as old age will let me.

Well, thou hast a son shall take this disgrace off me; scurvy, old, / filthy, scurvy lord! Well, I must be patient; there is no fettering of / authority. I'll beat him, by my life, if I can meet him with any / convenience, an he were double and double a lord. I'll have no more / pity of his age than I would have of—I'll beat him, and if I could but / meet him again.

Well, you have a son who will wipe this disgrace off me, you scabby, old, filthy, scabby lord! Well, I must be patient. There's no chaining up authority. I'll beat him, I swear on my life, if I can meet him at a good moment, even if he were twice as much a lord as he is. I'll have no more pity for his age than I would for... I'll beat him, if I could only meet him again.
Sirrah, your lord and master's married; there's news for you; you have / a new mistress.
Fellow, your lord and master is married. There's news for you: you have a new mistress.
I most unfeignedly beseech your lordship to make some reservation of / your wrongs. He is my good lord; whom I serve above is my master.
I most sincerely beg your lordship to hold back your insults. He is my good lord; the one I serve above is my master.

The devil it is that's thy master. Why dost thou garter up thy arms o' / this fashion? Dost make hose of thy sleeves? Do other servants so? Thou / wert best set thy lower part where thy nose stands. By mine honour, if / I were but two hours younger, I'd beat thee. Methink'st thou art a / general offence, and every man should beat thee. I think thou wast / created for men to breathe themselves upon thee.

The devil is your master. Why do you tie up your arms in this fashion? Are you making stockings of your sleeves? Do other servants do that? You'd better turn yourself upside down and put your backside where your nose is. On my honour, if I were just two hours younger, I'd beat you. You seem to me an offence to everyone, and every man should beat you. I think you were created for men to get their exercise on.
This is hard and undeserved measure, my lord.
This is harsh and undeserved treatment, my lord.

Go to, sir; you were beaten in Italy for picking a kernel out of a / pomegranate; you are a vagabond, and no true traveller. You are more / saucy with lords and honourable personages than the commission of your / birth and virtue gives you heraldry. You are not worth another word, / else I'd call you knave. I leave you.

Come off it, sir. You were beaten in Italy for stealing a seed out of a pomegranate. You're a tramp and no real traveller. You're cheekier with lords and honourable people than your birth and worth give you any right to be. You're not worth another word, or I'd call you a rogue. I'm leaving you.
Good, very good, it is so then. Good, very good; let it be conceal'd / awhile.
Good, very good, so that's how it is. Good, very good. Let it be kept quiet for a while.
Undone, and forfeited to cares for ever!
Ruined, and handed over to misery for ever!
Although before the solemn priest I have sworn, / I will not bed her.
Although I've sworn it in front of the solemn priest, I will not sleep with her.
O my Parolles, they have married me! / I'll to the Tuscan wars, and never bed her.
Oh, my Parolles, they've married me! I'll go to the Tuscan wars and never sleep with her.
France is a dog-hole, and it no more merits / The tread of a man's foot: to the wars!
France is a kennel, and it doesn't deserve a man's footstep any more. To the wars!
There's letters from my mother; what th' import is / I know not yet.
There are letters from my mother. I don't know yet what they say.

Ay, that would be known. To th' wars, my boy, to th' wars! / He wears his honour in a box unseen / That hugs his kicky-wicky here at home, / Spending his manly marrow in her arms, / Which should sustain the bound and high curvet / Of Mars's fiery steed. To other regions! / France is a stable; we that dwell in't, jades, / Therefore, to th' war!

Yes, that should be found out. To the wars, my boy, to the wars! A man who cuddles his little darling here at home keeps his honour hidden in a box, spending his manly strength in her arms, strength that should control the leaps and high bounds of Mars's fiery horse. To other countries! France is a stable, and we who live in it are worn-out nags. So, to the war!

It shall be so; I'll send her to my house, / Acquaint my mother with my hate to her, / And wherefore I am fled; write to the king / That which I durst not speak. His present gift / Shall furnish me to those Italian fields / Where noble fellows strike. War is no strife / To the dark house and the detested wife.

So be it. I'll send her to my house, tell my mother that I hate her and why I've run away, and write to the King what I didn't dare say to his face. His gift to me just now will equip me for those Italian battlefields where noble fellows fight. War is no trouble compared with a gloomy home and a hated wife.
Will this caprichio hold in thee, art sure?
Will this whim of yours last? Are you sure?
Go with me to my chamber and advise me. / I'll send her straight away. Tomorrow / I'll to the wars, she to her single sorrow.
Come with me to my room and advise me. I'll send her away at once. Tomorrow I go to the wars, and she to her lonely sorrow.
Why, these balls bound; there's noise in it. 'Tis hard: / A young man married is a man that's marr'd. / Therefore away, and leave her bravely; go. / The king has done you wrong; but hush 'tis so.
Why, these balls are bouncing; there's some life in this. It's hard: a young man married is a man ruined. So, away, and leave her bravely. Go. The King has done you wrong, but hush, that's how it is.
My mother greets me kindly: is she well?
My mother sends me kind greetings. Is she well?
She is not well, but yet she has her health; she's very merry, but yet / she is not well. But thanks be given, she's very well, and wants / nothing i' the world; but yet she is not well.
She's not well, and yet she has her health. She's very cheerful, and yet she's not well. But thank God, she's very well and wants for nothing in the world. And yet she's not well.
If she be very well, what does she ail that she's not very well?
If she's very well, what's wrong with her that she's not very well?
Truly, she's very well indeed, but for two things.
Honestly, she's very well indeed, except for two things.
One, that she's not in heaven, whither God send her quickly! The other, / that she's in earth, from whence God send her quickly!
One, that she's not in heaven, where God send her quickly! The other, that she's on earth, from where God send her quickly!
I hope, sir, I have your good will to have mine own good fortune.
I hope, sir, I have your good wishes to keep my own good luck.
You had my prayers to lead them on; and to keep them on, have them / still. O, my knave how does my old lady?
You had my prayers to bring it on, and you have them still to keep it going. Oh, my rogue, how is my old lady?
So that you had her wrinkles and I her money, I would she did as you / say.
If you had her wrinkles and I had her money, I'd wish she were as you say.

Marry, you are the wiser man; for many a man's tongue shakes out his / master's undoing. To say nothing, to do nothing, to know nothing, and / to have nothing, is to be a great part of your title; which is within a / very little of nothing.

Well, you're the wiser man, because many a man's tongue shakes out his master's ruin. To say nothing, do nothing, know nothing and have nothing makes up a great part of your title, which comes very close to nothing.
You should have said, sir, before a knave thou art a knave; that is / before me thou art a knave. This had been truth, sir.
You should have said, sir, "Before a rogue you are a rogue", that is, "Before me you are a rogue." That would have been the truth, sir.
Go to, thou art a witty fool; I have found thee.
Come on, you're a witty fool. I've found you out.
Did you find me in yourself, sir? or were you taught to find me? The / search, sir, was profitable; and much fool may you find in you, even to / the world's pleasure and the increase of laughter.
Did you find me in yourself, sir, or were you taught where to find me? The search was worth it, sir, and may you find plenty of fool in yourself, to the world's delight and the increase of laughter.

A good knave, i' faith, and well fed. / Madam, my lord will go away tonight; / A very serious business calls on him. / The great prerogative and right of love, / Which, as your due, time claims, he does acknowledge; / But puts it off to a compell'd restraint; / Whose want, and whose delay, is strew'd with sweets; / Which they distil now in the curbed time, / To make the coming hour o'erflow with joy / And pleasure drown the brim.

A good rogue, honestly, and well fed. Madam, my lord is going away tonight. Very serious business calls him away. He acknowledges the great privilege and right of love, which time now claims as your due, but he is forced to postpone it. Its absence and its delay are sweetened with pleasures, which are being distilled during this time of restraint, to make the hour to come overflow with joy and fill pleasure to the brim.
That you will take your instant leave o' the king, / And make this haste as your own good proceeding, / Strengthen'd with what apology you think / May make it probable need.
That you take leave of the King at once, and present this hurry as your own idea, backed with whatever excuse you think will make it seem necessary.
That, having this obtain'd, you presently / Attend his further pleasure.
That, once you've done this, you come to him at once for his further instructions.
In everything I wait upon his will.
I obey his will in everything.
But I hope your lordship thinks not him a soldier.
But I hope your lordship doesn't think he's a soldier.
Yes, my lord, and of very valiant approof.
Yes, my lord, and of proven courage.
You have it from his own deliverance.
You have that from his own account.
Then my dial goes not true; I took this lark for a bunting.
Then my clock is wrong. I took this lark for a common bunting.
I do assure you, my lord, he is very great in knowledge, and / accordingly valiant.
I assure you, my lord, he knows a great deal and is brave to match.

I have, then, sinned against his experience and transgressed against / his valour; and my state that way is dangerous, since I cannot yet find / in my heart to repent. Here he comes; I pray you make us friends; I / will pursue the amity.

Then I've sinned against his experience and offended against his courage, and my soul is in danger there, since I can't yet find it in my heart to repent. Here he comes. Please make us friends; I'll work at the friendship.
[To Bertram] These things shall be done, sir.
[To Bertram] These things will be done, sir.
Pray you, sir, who's his tailor?
Tell me, sir, who's his tailor?
O, I know him well, I, sir; he, sir, is a good workman, a very good / tailor.
Oh, I know him well, I do, sir. He's a good workman, sir, a very good tailor.
[Aside to Parolles] Is she gone to the king?
[Aside to Parolles] Has she gone to the King?
I have writ my letters, casketed my treasure, / Given order for our horses; and tonight, / When I should take possession of the bride, / End ere I do begin.
I've written my letters, locked up my valuables and ordered our horses. And tonight, when I should take possession of my bride, I'll end before I begin.

A good traveller is something at the latter end of a dinner; but one / that lies three-thirds and uses a known truth to pass a thousand / nothings with, should be once heard and thrice beaten.— God save you, / Captain.

A good traveller is worth something at the end of a dinner. But one who lies two-thirds of the time, and uses one known truth to pass off a thousand pieces of nonsense, should be heard once and beaten three times. God save you, Captain.
Is there any unkindness between my lord and you, monsieur?
Is there some bad feeling between my lord and you, monsieur?
I know not how I have deserved to run into my lord's displeasure.
I don't know how I've deserved to fall into my lord's displeasure.
You have made shift to run into 't, boots and spurs and all, like him / that leapt into the custard; and out of it you'll run again, rather / than suffer question for your residence.
You've managed to run into it, boots, spurs and all, like the clown who jumps into the custard at the feast; and you'll run out of it again rather than be asked why you're there.
It may be you have mistaken him, my lord.
Perhaps you've misjudged him, my lord.

And shall do so ever, though I took him at his prayers. Fare you well, / my lord; and believe this of me, there can be no kernal in this light / nut; the soul of this man is his clothes; trust him not in matter of / heavy consequence; I have kept of them tame, and know their natures. / Farewell, monsieur; I have spoken better of you than you have or will / to deserve at my hand; but we must do good against evil.

And I always will, even if I caught him at his prayers. Goodbye, my lord, and believe me: there can be no kernel in this light nut. This man's soul is his clothes. Don't trust him in any serious matter. I've kept creatures like him as pets and know their nature. Goodbye, monsieur. I've spoken better of you than you have deserved or ever will deserve from me, but we must return good for evil.
Why, do you not know him?
Yes, I do know him well; and common speech / Gives him a worthy pass. Here comes my clog.
Yes, I know him well, and people speak well of him. Here comes my ball and chain.
I have, sir, as I was commanded from you, / Spoke with the king, and have procur'd his leave / For present parting; only he desires / Some private speech with you.
Sir, as you ordered, I have spoken with the King and got his permission to leave at once. Only he wants to speak with you in private.

I shall obey his will. / You must not marvel, Helen, at my course, / Which holds not colour with the time, nor does / The ministration and required office / On my particular. Prepared I was not / For such a business; therefore am I found / So much unsettled: this drives me to entreat you; / That presently you take your way for home, / And rather muse than ask why I entreat you: / For my respects are better than they seem; / And my appointments have in them a need / Greater than shows itself at the first view / To you that know them not. This to my mother.

I'll obey his wishes. You mustn't be surprised, Helen, at what I'm doing, which doesn't suit the occasion, nor do I carry out the duties expected of me. I wasn't prepared for such a business, and so I'm very unsettled. This makes me ask you to set off for home at once, and to wonder rather than ask why I ask you, because my reasons are better than they look, and my business has a need in it greater than appears at first sight to you, who don't know about it. This is for my mother.
'Twill be two days ere I shall see you; so / I leave you to your wisdom.
It will be two days before I see you. So I leave you to your good sense.
Sir, I can nothing say / But that I am your most obedient servant.
Sir, I can say nothing except that I am your most obedient servant.
Come, come, no more of that.
Come, come, no more of that.
And ever shall / With true observance seek to eke out that / Wherein toward me my homely stars have fail'd / To equal my great fortune.
And I will always try, with loyal service, to make up for what my humble birth has failed to give me to match my great good fortune.
Let that go. / My haste is very great. Farewell; hie home.
Never mind that. I'm in a great hurry. Goodbye. Hurry home.
Well, what do you want to say?
I am not worthy of the wealth I owe; / Nor dare I say 'tis mine, and yet it is; / But, like a timorous thief, most fain would steal / What law does vouch mine own.
I'm not worthy of the wealth I own, and I don't dare say it's mine, and yet it is. But like a nervous thief, I'd very much like to steal what the law says is my own.
Something; and scarce so much; nothing indeed. / I would not tell you what I would, my lord. Faith, yes, / Strangers and foes do sunder and not kiss.
Something, and hardly even that: nothing, really. I'd rather not tell you what I want, my lord. Well, yes: strangers and enemies part without a kiss.
I pray you, stay not, but in haste to horse.
Please, don't wait, but hurry to your horse.
I shall not break your bidding, good my lord. / Where are my other men, monsieur? / Farewell,
I won't disobey you, my good lord. Where are my other servants, monsieur? Goodbye.
Go thou toward home, where I will never come / Whilst I can shake my sword or hear the drum. / Away, and for our flight.
You go home, where I will never come as long as I can wave a sword or hear a drum. Away, and let's make our escape.
So that, from point to point, now have you heard / The fundamental reasons of this war, / Whose great decision hath much blood let forth, / And more thirsts after.
So now you have heard, point by point, the basic reasons for this war, whose great outcome has already cost much blood and thirsts for more.
Holy seems the quarrel / Upon your Grace's part; black and fearful / On the opposer.
The quarrel seems holy on your Grace's side, and black and frightening on your enemy's.
Therefore we marvel much our cousin France / Would, in so just a business, shut his bosom / Against our borrowing prayers.
So we're very surprised that our cousin the King of France should, in so just a cause, close his heart against our requests for help.

Good my lord, / The reasons of our state I cannot yield, / But like a common and an outward man / That the great figure of a council frames / By self-unable motion; therefore dare not / Say what I think of it, since I have found / Myself in my incertain grounds to fail / As often as I guess'd.

My good lord, I can't explain the reasons of our state, except as an ordinary outsider who imagines the great workings of a council with no power of his own to understand them. So I don't dare say what I think about it, since I've found myself wrong every time I've guessed on such uncertain ground.
Let it be as he pleases.
But I am sure the younger of our nature, / That surfeit on their ease, will day by day / Come here for physic.
But I'm sure the younger men of our kind, who are sick of their easy life, will come here day by day for a cure.
Welcome shall they be; / And all the honours that can fly from us / Shall on them settle. You know your places well; / When better fall, for your avails they fell. / Tomorrow to the field.
They'll be welcome, and every honour I can give will settle on them. You know your positions well. When better ones fall vacant, they fall for your benefit. Tomorrow, to the battlefield.
It hath happen'd all as I would have had it, save that he comes not / along with her.
Everything has happened as I wanted, except that he isn't coming with her.
By my troth, I take my young lord to be a very melancholy man.
Honestly, I think my young lord is a very melancholy man.
By what observance, I pray you?
What makes you say so, may I ask?
Why, he will look upon his boot and sing; mend the ruff and sing; ask / questions and sing; pick his teeth and sing. I know a man that had this / trick of melancholy sold a goodly manor for a song.
Why, he looks at his boot and sings, straightens his collar and sings, asks questions and sings, picks his teeth and sings. I knew a man with this melancholy habit who sold a fine estate for a song.
Let me see what he writes, and when he means to come.
Let me see what he writes, and when he plans to come.

I have no mind to Isbel since I was at court. Our old lings and our / Isbels o' th' country are nothing like your old ling and your Isbels o' / th' court. The brains of my Cupid's knock'd out, and I begin to love, / as an old man loves money, with no stomach.

I've lost my taste for Isbel since I was at court. Our old salt fish and our Isbels in the country are nothing like your old salt fish and your Isbels at court. My Cupid's brains have been knocked out, and I'm starting to love the way an old man loves money: with no appetite.

[Reads] I have sent you a daughter-in-law; she hath recovered the / king and undone me. I have wedded her, not bedded her, and sworn to / make the "not" eternal. You shall hear I am run away; know it before / the report come. If there be breadth enough in the world, I will hold a / long distance. My duty to you. / Your unfortunate son, / BERTRAM.

[Reads] "I have sent you a daughter-in-law. She has cured the King and ruined me. I have married her but not slept with her, and I've sworn to make the 'not' last for ever. You'll hear that I have run away; know it before the news arrives. If the world is wide enough, I'll keep a long way off. My respects to you. Your unhappy son, Bertram."
This is not well, rash and unbridled boy, / To fly the favours of so good a king, / To pluck his indignation on thy head / By the misprizing of a maid too virtuous / For the contempt of empire.
This is wrong, you rash, uncontrolled boy, to run away from the favours of so good a king, and bring his anger down on your head by undervaluing a girl too virtuous to be scorned even by an emperor.
O madam, yonder is heavy news within between two soldiers and my young / lady.
Oh, madam, there's sad news in there, between two soldiers and my young lady.
Nay, there is some comfort in the news, some comfort; your son will not / be kill'd so soon as I thought he would.
No, there's some comfort in the news, some comfort: your son won't be killed as soon as I thought.

So say I, madam, if he run away, as I hear he does; the danger is in / standing to't; that's the loss of men, though it be the getting of / children. Here they come will tell you more. For my part, I only hear / your son was run away.

That's what I say, madam, if he runs away, as I hear he does. The danger is in standing your ground: that's what loses men, though it's also what gets children. Here come people who will tell you more. For my part, I only hear that your son has run away.
Madam, my lord is gone, for ever gone.
Madam, my lord is gone, gone for ever.
Think upon patience. Pray you, gentlemen,— / I have felt so many quirks of joy and grief / That the first face of neither on the start / Can woman me unto 't. Where is my son, I pray you?
Think about patience. Please, gentlemen: I have felt so many sudden turns of joy and grief that neither one can make me cry like a woman at first sight. Where is my son, please?
Madam, he's gone to serve the Duke of Florence; / We met him thitherward, for thence we came, / And, after some despatch in hand at court, / Thither we bend again.
Madam, he's gone to serve the Duke of Florence. We met him on his way there, because that's where we came from, and once we've done some business at court we're heading back there.
Look on this letter, madam; here's my passport.
Look at this letter, madam. Here's my passport.

[Reads] When thou canst get the ring upon my finger, which never / shall come off, and show me a child begotten of thy body that I am / father to, then call me husband; but in such a "then" I write a / "never". / This is a dreadful sentence.

[Reads] "When you can get the ring from my finger, which will never come off, and show me a child born from your body that I am the father of, then call me husband. But in such a 'then' I write a 'never'." This is a terrible sentence.
Did you bring this letter, gentlemen?
Ay, madam; And for the contents' sake, are sorry for our pains.
Yes, madam, and because of what's in it, we're sorry we took the trouble.

I pr'ythee, lady, have a better cheer; / If thou engrossest all the griefs are thine, / Thou robb'st me of a moiety. He was my son, / But I do wash his name out of my blood, / And thou art all my child. Towards Florence is he?
Please, lady, cheer up. If you take all the griefs on yourself, you rob me of my half. He was my son, but I wash his name out of my blood, and you are my only child. Is he going to Florence?
Such is his noble purpose, and, believe't, / The duke will lay upon him all the honour / That good convenience claims.
That's his noble intention, and believe me, the Duke will give him all the honour that's fitting.
Ay, madam, with the swiftest wing of speed.
Yes, madam, as fast as we can fly.
[Reads] Till I have no wife, I have nothing in France. / 'Tis bitter.
[Reads] "Until I have no wife, I have nothing in France." That's bitter.
'Tis but the boldness of his hand haply, which his heart was not / consenting to.
Perhaps it's just his hand being bold, and his heart didn't agree.

Nothing in France until he have no wife! / There's nothing here that is too good for him / But only she, and she deserves a lord / That twenty such rude boys might tend upon, / And call her hourly mistress. Who was with him?

Nothing in France until he has no wife! There's nothing here that is too good for him except her, and she deserves a lord whom twenty rude boys like him should serve and call her mistress every hour. Who was with him?
A servant only, and a gentleman which I have sometime known.
Only a servant, and a gentleman I once knew.
A very tainted fellow, and full of wickedness. / My son corrupts a well-derived nature / With his inducement.
A thoroughly corrupt fellow, full of wickedness. My son spoils his good inherited nature by listening to him.
Indeed, good lady, / The fellow has a deal of that too much, / Which holds him much to have.
Indeed, good lady, the fellow has a great deal too much of that wickedness, which serves him very well.
Y'are welcome, gentlemen. / I will entreat you, when you see my son, / To tell him that his sword can never win / The honour that he loses: more I'll entreat you / Written to bear along.
You're welcome, gentlemen. I'll ask you, when you see my son, to tell him that his sword can never win back the honour he is losing. I'll ask you to take more of my message in writing.
We serve you, madam, / In that and all your worthiest affairs.
We are at your service, madam, in that and in all your most worthy business.
Not so, but as we change our courtesies. / Will you draw near?
Not that, but only as we exchange kindnesses. Will you come with me?

"Till I have no wife, I have nothing in France." / Nothing in France until he has no wife! / Thou shalt have none, Rossillon, none in France; / Then hast thou all again. Poor lord, is't I / That chase thee from thy country, and expose / Those tender limbs of thine to the event / Of the none-sparing war? And is it I / That drive thee from the sportive court, where thou / Wast shot at with fair eyes, to be the mark / Of smoky muskets? O you leaden messengers, / That ride upon the violent speed of fire, / Fly with false aim; move the still-peering air, / That sings with piercing; do not touch my lord. / Whoever shoots at him, I set him there; / Whoever charges on his forward breast, / I am the caitiff that do hold him to't; / And though I kill him not, I am the cause / His death was so effected. Better 'twere / I met the ravin lion when he roar'd / With sharp constraint of hunger; better 'twere / That all the miseries which nature owes / Were mine at once. No; come thou home, Rossillon, / Whence honour but of danger wins a scar, / As oft it loses all. I will be gone; / My being here it is that holds thee hence. / Shall I stay here to do't? No, no, although / The air of paradise did fan the house, / And angels offic'd all. I will be gone, / That pitiful rumour may report my flight / To consolate thine ear. Come, night; end, day; / For with the dark, poor thief, I'll steal away.

"Until I have no wife, I have nothing in France." Nothing in France until he has no wife! You'll have none, Rossillon, none in France; then you'll have everything again. Poor lord, is it me who is chasing you out of your country, and exposing your tender body to the chances of merciless war? And is it me who drives you from the playful court, where beautiful eyes shot at you, to be the target of smoking muskets? Oh, you lead bullets that ride on the violent speed of fire, fly wide of your aim! Pierce the air that whistles as you cut through it, and closes up behind you; don't touch my lord. Whoever shoots at him, I put him there; whoever charges at his brave chest, I'm the wretch who holds him to it. And though I don't kill him, I'm the cause of his death if it happens. It would be better for me to meet the ravenous lion when he roars with the sharp pain of hunger; better that all the miseries nature has to give were mine at once. No: come home, Rossillon, from where honour wins only a scar from danger, and often loses everything. I'll go. It's my being here that keeps you away. Shall I stay here and do that? No, no, even if the air of paradise cooled the house and angels did all the work. I'll go, so that rumour can pityingly report my running away and comfort your ears. Come, night; end, day; because with the dark I'll steal away like a poor thief.
The general of our horse thou art, and we, / Great in our hope, lay our best love and credence / Upon thy promising fortune.
You are general of our cavalry, and we, full of hope, place our deepest love and trust in your promising fortune.
Sir, it is / A charge too heavy for my strength; but yet / We'll strive to bear it for your worthy sake / To th'extreme edge of hazard.
Sir, it's a responsibility too heavy for my strength, but we'll do our best to carry it, for your worthy sake, to the very edge of danger.
Then go thou forth; / And fortune play upon thy prosperous helm, / As thy auspicious mistress!
Then go out, and may Fortune smile on your successful helmet like a lucky mistress!
This very day, / Great Mars, I put myself into thy file; / Make me but like my thoughts, and I shall prove / A lover of thy drum, hater of love.
This very day, great Mars, I join your ranks. Only make me as good as my thoughts, and I'll prove a lover of your drum and a hater of love.
Alas! and would you take the letter of her? / Might you not know she would do as she has done, / By sending me a letter? Read it again.
Oh no! And did you take the letter from her? Couldn't you tell she would do what she has done, if she was sending me a letter? Read it again.

[Reads] I am Saint Jaques' pilgrim, thither gone. / Ambitious love hath so in me offended / That barefoot plod I the cold ground upon, / With sainted vow my faults to have amended. / Write, write, that from the bloody course of war / My dearest master, your dear son, may hie. / Bless him at home in peace, whilst I from far / His name with zealous fervour sanctify. / His taken labours bid him me forgive; / I, his despiteful Juno, sent him forth / From courtly friends, with camping foes to live, / Where death and danger dog the heels of worth. / He is too good and fair for death and me; / Whom I myself embrace to set him free.

[Reads] "I'm a pilgrim of Saint Jaques, and gone there. My ambitious love has sinned so badly that I'm trudging barefoot on the cold ground, with a holy vow to have my faults put right. Write, write, so that my dearest master, your dear son, may hurry home from the bloody course of war. Bless him at home in peace, while I, far away, honour his name with my devoted prayers. Tell him to forgive me for the hardships he has taken on. I, his cruel Juno, sent him away from his friends at court to live among enemies in camp, where death and danger chase at the heels of the brave. He is too good and too handsome for death and me. I embrace death myself to set him free."

Ah, what sharp stings are in her mildest words! / Rynaldo, you did never lack advice so much / As letting her pass so; had I spoke with her, / I could have well diverted her intents, / Which thus she hath prevented.

Ah, what sharp stings there are in her gentlest words! Rinaldo, you never showed such poor judgement as letting her go like that. If I had spoken with her, I could easily have turned her from her plans, which she has now got ahead of.
Pardon me, madam; / If I had given you this at over-night, / She might have been o'erta'en; and yet she writes / Pursuit would be but vain.
Forgive me, madam. If I had given you this last night, she might have been caught up with. And yet she writes that chasing her would be useless.

What angel shall / Bless this unworthy husband? He cannot thrive, / Unless her prayers, whom heaven delights to hear / And loves to grant, reprieve him from the wrath / Of greatest justice. Write, write, Rynaldo, / To this unworthy husband of his wife; / Let every word weigh heavy of her worth, / That he does weigh too light; my greatest grief, / Though little he do feel it, set down sharply. / Dispatch the most convenient messenger. / When haply he shall hear that she is gone / He will return; and hope I may that she, / Hearing so much, will speed her foot again, / Led hither by pure love. Which of them both / Is dearest to me I have no skill in sense / To make distinction. Provide this messenger. / My heart is heavy, and mine age is weak; / Grief would have tears, and sorrow bids me speak.

What angel will bless this unworthy husband? He can't prosper unless her prayers, which heaven delights to hear and loves to grant, save him from the anger of the highest justice. Write, write, Rinaldo, to this husband unworthy of his wife. Let every word weigh heavy with her worth, which he values too lightly. Write down sharply my great grief, though he feels it little. Send the quickest messenger. Perhaps when he hears she has gone he will come back, and I can hope that she, hearing that, will hurry back here too, led by pure love. Which of them is dearer to me I can't tell. Get this messenger ready. My heart is heavy, and my age is weak. Grief wants tears, and sorrow makes me speak.
Nay, come; for if they do approach the city, we shall lose all the / sight.
No, come on, because if they get to the city we'll miss the whole show.
They say the French count has done most honourable service.
They say the French count has done very honourable service.
It is reported that he has taken their great'st commander, and that / with his own hand he slew the duke's brother.
It's reported that he has captured their most important commander, and killed the Duke's brother with his own hand.
We have lost our labour; they are gone a contrary way. Hark! you may / know by their trumpets.
We've wasted our effort; they've gone the other way. Listen! You can tell by their trumpets.
Come, let's return again, and suffice ourselves with the report of it. / Well, Diana, take heed of this French earl; the honour of a maid is her / name; and no legacy is so rich as honesty.
Come, let's go back and be content with hearing about it. Well, Diana, watch out for this French count. A girl's honour is her good name, and no inheritance is as rich as chastity.
I have told my neighbour how you have been solicited by a gentleman his / companion.
I've told my neighbour how you've been pestered by a gentleman, his companion.

I know that knave; hang him! one Parolles; a filthy officer he is in / those suggestions for the young earl. Beware of them, Diana; their / promises, enticements, oaths, tokens, and all these engines of lust, / are not the things they go under; many a maid hath been seduced by / them; and the misery is, example, that so terrible shows in the wreck / of maidenhood, cannot for all that dissuade succession, but that they / are limed with the twigs that threaten them. I hope I need not to / advise you further; but I hope your own grace will keep you where you / are, though there were no further danger known but the modesty which is / so lost.

I know that rogue, hang him! A man called Parolles: a filthy go-between for the young count in these proposals. Watch out for them, Diana. Their promises, temptations, oaths, love tokens and all these weapons of lust are not what they pretend to be. Many a girl has been seduced by them; and the misery of it is that the example, which looks so terrible in the wreck of a girl's virginity, still can't stop others following, but they're caught in the very traps that threaten them. I hope I don't need to advise you further, and I hope your own goodness will keep you as you are, even if the only danger were the loss of modesty.
You shall not need to fear me.
I hope so. Look, here comes a pilgrim. I know she will lie at my house; / thither they send one another; I'll question her. God save you, / pilgrim! Whither are bound?
I hope so. Look, here comes a pilgrim. I'm sure she'll stay at my house; they send each other there. I'll ask her. God save you, pilgrim! Where are you heading?
To Saint Jaques le Grand. / Where do the palmers lodge, I do beseech you?
To Saint Jaques the Great. Where do the pilgrims stay, please?
At the Saint Francis here, beside the port.
At the Saint Francis inn here, beside the gate.

Ay, marry, is't. Hark you, they come this way. / If you will tarry, holy pilgrim, / But till the troops come by, / I will conduct you where you shall be lodg'd; / The rather for I think I know your hostess / As ample as myself.

Yes, it is indeed. Listen, they're coming this way. If you'll wait, holy pilgrim, just until the troops go by, I'll take you to where you'll stay, all the more since I think I know your landlady as well as I know myself.
If you shall please so, pilgrim.
I thank you, and will stay upon your leisure.
Thank you. I'll wait until you're ready.
You came, I think, from France?
You've come from France, I think?
Here you shall see a countryman of yours / That has done worthy service.
Here you'll see a countryman of yours who has done fine service.
The Count Rossillon. Know you such a one?
The Count of Rossillon. Do you know him?
But by the ear, that hears most nobly of him; / His face I know not.
Only by hearsay, and I hear very well of him. I don't know his face.
Whatsome'er he is, / He's bravely taken here. He stole from France, / As 'tis reported, for the king had married him / Against his liking. Think you it is so?
Whatever he is, he's thought very highly of here. He ran away from France, they say, because the King married him against his will. Do you think that's true?
Ay, surely, mere the truth; I know his lady.
Yes, certainly, the plain truth. I know his wife.
There is a gentleman that serves the count / Reports but coarsely of her.
There's a gentleman who serves the count who speaks very rudely of her.

O, I believe with him, / In argument of praise, or to the worth / Of the great count himself, she is too mean / To have her name repeated; all her deserving / Is a reserved honesty, and that / I have not heard examin'd.

Oh, I agree with him that, when it comes to praise, or compared with the worth of the great count himself, she's too low to have her name mentioned. All her merit is a modest chastity, and I haven't heard that questioned.
Alas, poor lady! / 'Tis a hard bondage to become the wife / Of a detesting lord.
Oh, poor lady! It's a hard slavery to be the wife of a lord who hates you.
Ay, right; good creature, wheresoe'er she is, / Her heart weighs sadly. This young maid might do her / A shrewd turn, if she pleas'd.
Yes, that's right. The good creature, wherever she is, her heart must be sad. This young girl could do her a nasty turn if she wanted.
How do you mean? / Maybe the amorous count solicits her / In the unlawful purpose.
What do you mean? Perhaps the lovesick count is chasing her for an unlawful purpose?
He does indeed, / And brokes with all that can in such a suit / Corrupt the tender honour of a maid; / But she is arm'd for him, and keeps her guard / In honestest defence.
He is indeed, and he's bargaining with everything that, in such wooing, can corrupt a girl's tender honour. But she is armed against him and keeps up her guard in the most honest defence.
So, now they come. / That is Antonio, the Duke's eldest son; / That Escalus.
So, here they come now. That's Antonio, the Duke's eldest son; that's Escalus.
He; / That with the plume; 'tis a most gallant fellow. / I would he lov'd his wife; if he were honester / He were much goodlier. Is't not a handsome gentleman?
Him, with the feather. He's a most dashing fellow. I wish he loved his wife. If he were more honest he'd be much better looking. Isn't he a handsome gentleman?
'Tis pity he is not honest. Yond's that same knave / That leads him to these places. Were I his lady / I would poison that vile rascal.
It's a pity he isn't honest. That's the same rogue over there who leads him to these places. If I were his wife I'd poison that vile scoundrel.
That jack-an-apes with scarfs. Why is he melancholy?
That monkey with the scarves. Why is he so gloomy?
Perchance he's hurt i' the battle.
Perhaps he was hurt in the battle.
He's shrewdly vex'd at something. Look, he has spied us.
He's badly upset about something. Look, he's seen us.
And your courtesy, for a ring-carrier!
And your fine manners too, you pimp!
The troop is past. Come, pilgrim, I will bring you / Where you shall host; of enjoin'd penitents / There's four or five, to great Saint Jaques bound, / Already at my house.
The soldiers have gone past. Come, pilgrim, I'll take you to where you'll stay. There are four or five penitents already at my house, on their way to great Saint Jaques.

I humbly thank you. / Please it this matron and this gentle maid / To eat with us tonight; the charge and thanking / Shall be for me; and, to requite you further, / I will bestow some precepts of this virgin, / Worthy the note.

Thank you humbly. If this lady and this gentle girl would eat with us tonight, the cost and the thanks will be mine. And to repay you further, I'll give some advice about this young woman that's worth hearing.
Nay, good my lord, put him to't; let him have his way.
No, my good lord, put him to the test. Let him do it his way.
If your lordship find him not a hilding, hold me no more in your / respect.
If your lordship doesn't find him a good-for-nothing, stop respecting me.
On my life, my lord, a bubble.
On my life, my lord, he's a bubble.
Do you think I am so far deceived in him?
Do you think I'm so badly deceived in him?

Believe it, my lord, in mine own direct knowledge, without any malice, / but to speak of him as my kinsman, he's a most notable coward, an / infinite and endless liar, an hourly promise-breaker, the owner of no / one good quality worthy your lordship's entertainment.

Believe it, my lord. I know it directly, without any malice, and speak of him as if he were my own relative: he's a notorious coward, an infinite and endless liar, a promise-breaker every hour, and has not one good quality worth your lordship's notice.
It were fit you knew him; lest, reposing too far in his virtue, which / he hath not, he might at some great and trusty business, in a main / danger fail you.
You ought to know him, in case you rely too much on a virtue he doesn't have, and he lets you down in some great and important business, in serious danger.
I would I knew in what particular action to try him.
I wish I knew some particular action to test him with.
None better than to let him fetch off his drum, which you hear him so / confidently undertake to do.
Nothing better than letting him go and recover his drum, which you heard him so confidently promise to do.

I with a troop of Florentines will suddenly surprise him; such I will / have whom I am sure he knows not from the enemy; we will bind and / hoodwink him so that he shall suppose no other but that he is carried / into the leaguer of the adversaries when we bring him to our own tents. / Be but your lordship present at his examination; if he do not for the / promise of his life, and in the highest compulsion of base fear, offer / to betray you, and deliver all the intelligence in his power against / you, and that with the divine forfeit of his soul upon oath, never / trust my judgment in anything.

I'll ambush him suddenly with a troop of Florentines, men I'm sure he can't tell apart from the enemy. We'll tie him up and blindfold him, so that he'll think he's being carried into the enemy camp when we take him to our own tents. Just be there, your lordship, when we question him. If he doesn't, for the promise of his life and driven by the lowest fear, offer to betray you and tell all he knows against you, and swear it on his immortal soul, never trust my judgement in anything again.

O, for the love of laughter, let him fetch his drum; he says he has a / stratagem for't. When your lordship sees the bottom of his success / in't, and to what metal this counterfeit lump of ore will be melted, if / you give him not John Drum's entertainment, your inclining cannot be / removed. Here he comes.

Oh, for the love of laughter, let him fetch his drum; he says he has a plan for it. When your lordship sees how his success turns out, and what metal this fake lump of ore melts down to, if you don't give him a good drumming out, your liking for him can never be shifted. Here he comes.
O, for the love of laughter, hinder not the honour of his design: let / him fetch off his drum in any hand.
Oh, for the love of laughter, don't get in the way of his honourable plan. Let him fetch his drum by any means.
How now, monsieur! This drum sticks sorely in your disposition.
Hello, monsieur! This drum sticks badly in your mind.
A pox on 't; let it go; 'tis but a drum.
To hell with it, let it go. It's only a drum.
But a drum! Is't but a drum? A drum so lost! There was excellent / command, to charge in with our horse upon our own wings, and to rend / our own soldiers.
Only a drum! Is it only a drum? A drum lost like that! That was a fine command, to charge our cavalry into our own wings and tear apart our own soldiers!
That was not to be blam'd in the command of the service; it was a / disaster of war that Caesar himself could not have prevented, if he had / been there to command.
The commanders weren't to blame for that. It was a disaster of war that Caesar himself couldn't have prevented if he had been in command.
Well, we cannot greatly condemn our success: some dishonour we had in / the loss of that drum, but it is not to be recovered.
Well, we can't complain much about how it went. We had some disgrace in losing that drum, but it can't be recovered.
It might, but it is not now.
It might, but it can't be now.
It is to be recovered. But that the merit of service is seldom / attributed to the true and exact performer, I would have that drum or / another, or hic jacet.
It can be recovered. If it weren't that credit for service is so rarely given to the man who actually does it, I'd have that drum or another one, or "here lies" on my gravestone.

Why, if you have a stomach, to't, monsieur, if you think your mystery / in stratagem can bring this instrument of honour again into his native / quarter, be magnanimous in the enterprise, and go on; I will grace the / attempt for a worthy exploit; if you speed well in it, the duke shall / both speak of it and extend to you what further becomes his greatness, / even to the utmost syllable of your worthiness.

Why, if you have the appetite for it, go to it, monsieur. If you think your skill in strategy can bring this symbol of honour back to its proper quarters, be bold in the attempt and go ahead. I'll honour the attempt as a worthy exploit. If you succeed, the Duke will both speak of it and give you whatever further reward suits his greatness, to the last syllable of what you deserve.
By the hand of a soldier, I will undertake it.
On a soldier's hand, I'll do it.
But you must not now slumber in it.
But you mustn't go to sleep on it now.
I'll about it this evening; and I will presently pen down my dilemmas, / encourage myself in my certainty, put myself into my mortal / preparation; and by midnight look to hear further from me.
I'll be about it this evening. I'll write down my plans at once, encourage myself in my certainty and prepare myself for death. Expect to hear more from me by midnight.
May I be bold to acquaint his grace you are gone about it?
May I tell his grace that you have gone about it?
I know not what the success will be, my lord, but the attempt I vow.
I don't know how it will turn out, my lord, but I swear I'll attempt it.
I know th'art valiant; and to the possibility of thy soldiership, will / subscribe for thee. Farewell.
I know you're brave, and I'll vouch for your soldiership to the limit of its possibility. Goodbye.

No more than a fish loves water. Is not this a strange fellow, my lord, / that so confidently seems to undertake this business, which he knows is / not to be done; damns himself to do, and dares better be damn'd than to / do't.

No more than a fish likes water. Isn't this a strange fellow, my lord, to seem so confident in taking on this business, which he knows can't be done? He damns himself by swearing to do it, and would rather be damned than do it.

You do not know him, my lord, as we do; certain it is that he will / steal himself into a man's favour, and for a week escape a great deal / of discoveries, but when you find him out, you have him ever after.
You don't know him as we do, my lord. It's certain that he can creep into a man's favour and for a week avoid being found out, but once you've found him out, you have him for ever after.
Why, do you think he will make no deed at all of this, that so / seriously he does address himself unto?
Why, do you think he won't do anything at all about this, when he commits himself to it so seriously?

None in the world; but return with an invention, and clap upon you two / or three probable lies; but we have almost embossed him; you shall see / his fall tonight; for indeed he is not for your lordship's respect.

Nothing in the world, except come back with a made-up story and hit you with two or three likely lies. But we've almost run him to ground. You'll see his fall tonight, because really he doesn't deserve your lordship's respect.

We'll make you some sport with the fox ere we case him. He was first / smok'd by the old Lord Lafew; when his disguise and he is parted, tell / me what a sprat you shall find him; which you shall see this very / night.

We'll give you some fun with the fox before we skin him. He was first sniffed out by old Lord Lafew. When his disguise and he are separated, tell me what a little fish you find him. You'll see it this very night.
I must go look my twigs. He shall be caught.
I must go and set my traps. He'll be caught.
Your brother, he shall go along with me.
Your brother can come with me.
As't please your lordship. I'll leave you.
As your lordship pleases. I'll leave you.
Now will I lead you to the house, and show you / The lass I spoke of.
Now I'll take you to the house and show you the girl I spoke about.

That's all the fault. I spoke with her but once, / And found her wondrous cold, but I sent to her / By this same coxcomb that we have i' the wind / Tokens and letters which she did re-send, / And this is all I have done. She's a fair creature; / Will you go see her?

That's her only fault. I spoke to her only once, and found her amazingly cold. But I sent her love tokens and letters through this same fool we're hunting, and she sent them back. That's all I've done. She's a beautiful creature. Will you come and see her?
With all my heart, my lord.
With all my heart, my lord.
If you misdoubt me that I am not she, / I know not how I shall assure you further, / But I shall lose the grounds I work upon.
If you doubt that I am who I say, I don't know how I can convince you further without losing the ground my plan stands on.
Though my estate be fall'n, I was well born, / Nothing acquainted with these businesses, / And would not put my reputation now / In any staining act.
Though I've come down in the world, I was born a gentlewoman. I know nothing of these sorts of business, and I wouldn't risk my reputation now on any act that might stain it.

Nor would I wish you. / First give me trust, the count he is my husband, / And what to your sworn counsel I have spoken / Is so from word to word; and then you cannot, / By the good aid that I of you shall borrow, / Err in bestowing it.

Nor would I want you to. First, believe that the count is my husband, and that what I've told you under your oath of secrecy is true, word for word. Then you can't go wrong in giving me the good help I'll borrow from you.
I should believe you, / For you have show'd me that which well approves / Y'are great in fortune.
I believe you, because you've shown me enough to prove you're a woman of great fortune.

Take this purse of gold, / And let me buy your friendly help thus far, / Which I will over-pay, and pay again / When I have found it. The count he woos your daughter / Lays down his wanton siege before her beauty, / Resolv'd to carry her; let her in fine consent, / As we'll direct her how 'tis best to bear it. / Now his important blood will naught deny / That she'll demand; a ring the county wears, / That downward hath succeeded in his house / From son to son, some four or five descents / Since the first father wore it. This ring he holds / In most rich choice; yet, in his idle fire, / To buy his will, it would not seem too dear, / Howe'er repented after.

Take this purse of gold, and let me buy your friendly help so far. I'll pay you more, and pay you again, once I have it. The count is wooing your daughter, laying his lustful siege to her beauty, determined to conquer her. Let her finally agree, and we'll tell her the best way to handle it. His urgent desire won't refuse anything she asks for. The count wears a ring that has been handed down in his family from son to son for four or five generations since the first ancestor wore it. He values this ring very highly. Yet in his foolish passion, to get what he wants, it won't seem too high a price, however much he regrets it afterwards.
Now I see / The bottom of your purpose.
Now I see what you're aiming at.

You see it lawful then; it is no more / But that your daughter, ere she seems as won, / Desires this ring; appoints him an encounter; / In fine, delivers me to fill the time, / Herself most chastely absent. After, / To marry her, I'll add three thousand crowns / To what is pass'd already.

Then you see it's lawful. It's only that your daughter, before she seems to give in, asks for this ring and arranges to meet him; and in the end hands me over to take her place, while she herself stays chastely away. Afterwards, for her marriage, I'll add three thousand crowns to what I've already given.

I have yielded. / Instruct my daughter how she shall persever, / That time and place with this deceit so lawful / May prove coherent. Every night he comes / With musics of all sorts, and songs compos'd / To her unworthiness: it nothing steads us / To chide him from our eaves; for he persists / As if his life lay on 't.

I agree. Teach my daughter how to behave so that time and place fit this lawful trick. Every night he comes with all kinds of music, and songs written about her unworthy self. It does us no good to scold him away from under our windows, because he persists as if his life depended on it.

Why then tonight / Let us assay our plot; which, if it speed, / Is wicked meaning in a lawful deed, / And lawful meaning in a lawful act, / Where both not sin, and yet a sinful fact. / But let's about it.

Why then, tonight let's try our plan. If it succeeds, it is a wicked intention in a lawful deed and a lawful intention in a lawful act: neither of them sins, and yet the deed looks sinful. But let's get to it.

He can come no other way but by this hedge-corner. When you sally upon / him, speak what terrible language you will; though you understand it / not yourselves, no matter; for we must not seem to understand him, / unless someone among us, whom we must produce for an interpreter.

He can't come any other way but past this corner of the hedge. When you jump out at him, speak whatever terrible language you like. It doesn't matter if you don't understand it yourselves, because we mustn't seem to understand him, except for one of us, whom we'll set up as an interpreter.
Good captain, let me be th' interpreter.
Good captain, let me be the interpreter.
Art not acquainted with him? Knows he not thy voice?
Don't you know him? Doesn't he know your voice?
But what linsey-woolsey has thou to speak to us again?
But what mixed-up gibberish will you speak back to us?
E'en such as you speak to me.
The same kind you speak to me.

He must think us some band of strangers i' the adversary's / entertainment. Now he hath a smack of all neighbouring languages, / therefore we must every one be a man of his own fancy; not to know what / we speak one to another, so we seem to know, is to know straight our / purpose: choughs' language, gabble enough, and good enough. As for you, / interpreter, you must seem very politic. But couch, ho! Here he comes; / to beguile two hours in a sleep, and then to return and swear the lies / he forges.

He must think we're some band of foreign soldiers in the enemy's pay. Now, he has a taste of all the neighbouring languages, so each of us must make up his own. As long as we seem to understand each other, not knowing what we're saying to one another serves our purpose perfectly: jackdaw talk, gabble enough, and good enough. As for you, interpreter, you must look very cunning. But down, hide! Here he comes, to waste two hours sleeping, and then go back and swear to the lies he makes up.

Ten o'clock. Within these three hours 'twill be time enough to go home. / What shall I say I have done? It must be a very plausive invention that / carries it. They begin to smoke me, and disgraces have of late knock'd / too often at my door. I find my tongue is too foolhardy, but my heart / hath the fear of Mars before it, and of his creatures, not daring the / reports of my tongue.

Ten o'clock. In three hours it'll be late enough to go home. What shall I say I've done? It will have to be a very convincing story to get away with it. They're starting to smell me out, and disgrace has knocked at my door too often lately. I find my tongue is too reckless, but my heart is afraid of Mars and his soldiers, and doesn't dare do what my tongue promises.
[Aside] This is the first truth that e'er thine own tongue was / guilty of.
[Aside] That's the first truth your tongue was ever guilty of.

What the devil should move me to undertake the recovery of this drum, / being not ignorant of the impossibility, and knowing I had no such / purpose? I must give myself some hurts, and say I got them in exploit; / yet slight ones will not carry it. They will say "Came you off with so / little?" and great ones I dare not give. Wherefore, what's the / instance? Tongue, I must put you into a butter-woman's mouth, and buy / myself another of Bajazet's mule, if you prattle me into these perils.

What the devil made me take on recovering this drum, when I knew it was impossible and I had no intention of doing it? I must give myself some wounds and say I got them in action. But small ones won't do it. They'll say, "Did you get off so lightly?" And I don't dare give myself big ones. So what's the proof to be? Tongue, I'll have to put you in a milkmaid's mouth and buy myself a mule's tongue instead, if you chatter me into these dangers.
[Aside] Is it possible he should know what he is, and be that he is?
[Aside] Is it possible he can know what he is, and still be what he is?
I would the cutting of my garments would serve the turn, or the / breaking of my Spanish sword.
I wish cutting my clothes would do the trick, or breaking my Spanish sword.
[Aside] We can't let you off like that.
Or the baring of my beard, and to say it was in stratagem.
Or shaving off my beard, and saying it was part of a strategy.
Or to drown my clothes, and say I was stripped.
Or soaking my clothes, and saying I was stripped.
Though I swore I leap'd from the window of the citadel,—
Even if I swore I jumped from the citadel window...
[Aside] Three great oaths would scarce make that be believed.
[Aside] Three great oaths would hardly make anyone believe that.
I would I had any drum of the enemy's; I would swear I recover'd it.
I wish I had any drum of the enemy's. I'd swear I recovered it.
[Aside] You'll hear one in a moment.
A drum now of the enemy's!
Cargo, cargo, cargo, villianda par corbo, cargo.
Cargo, cargo, cargo, villianda par corbo, cargo.
O, ransom, ransom! Do not hide mine eyes.
Oh, ransom, ransom! Don't cover my eyes.

I know you are the Muskos' regiment, / And I shall lose my life for want of language. / If there be here German, or Dane, Low Dutch, / Italian, or French, let him speak to me, / I'll discover that which shall undo the Florentine.

I know you're the Muskos regiment, and I'll lose my life because I can't speak the language. If there's anyone here who speaks German or Danish, Dutch, Italian or French, let him speak to me. I'll reveal what will ruin the Florentines.
Boskos vauvado. I understand thee, and can speak thy tongue. / Kerelybonto. Sir, Betake thee to thy faith, for seventeen poniards / are at thy bosom.
Boskos vauvado. I understand you and can speak your language. Kerelybonto. Sir, say your prayers, because seventeen daggers are at your chest.
O, pray, pray, pray! / Manka revania dulche.
Oh, pray, pray, pray! Manka revania dulche.
The General is content to spare thee yet; / And, hoodwink'd as thou art, will lead thee on / To gather from thee. Haply thou mayst inform / Something to save thy life.
The General agrees to spare you for now, and will lead you away blindfolded as you are, to get information out of you. Perhaps you can tell something to save your life.
O, let me live, / And all the secrets of our camp I'll show, / Their force, their purposes; nay, I'll speak that / Which you will wonder at.
Oh, let me live, and I'll reveal all the secrets of our camp, their strength, their plans. Yes, I'll tell you things that will amaze you.
But will you do it truthfully?
If I do not, damn me.
Acordo linta. / Come on; thou art granted space.
Acordo linta. Come on. You're given time.
Go tell the Count Rossillon and my brother / We have caught the woodcock, and will keep him muffled / Till we do hear from them.
Go and tell the Count of Rossillon and my brother that we've caught the woodcock and will keep him blindfolded until we hear from them.
'A will betray us all unto ourselves; / Inform on that.
He will betray all of us to ourselves. Tell them that.
Till then I'll keep him dark, and safely lock'd.
Until then I'll keep him in the dark and safely locked up.
They told me that your name was Fontybell.
They told me your name was Fontibell.

Titled goddess; / And worth it, with addition! But, fair soul, / In your fine frame hath love no quality? / If the quick fire of youth light not your mind, / You are no maiden but a monument; / When you are dead, you should be such a one / As you are now; for you are cold and stern, / And now you should be as your mother was / When your sweet self was got.

Named after a goddess, and worth it, and more! But, beautiful soul, is there no love at all in your lovely body? If the lively fire of youth doesn't light up your mind, you're not a girl but a statue on a tomb. When you're dead you should be as you are now, because now you're cold and hard. Now you should be as your mother was when your sweet self was conceived.
No. / My mother did but duty; such, my lord, / As you owe to your wife.
No. My mother was only doing her duty, the same duty, my lord, that you owe your wife.
No more a' that! / I pr'ythee do not strive against my vows; / I was compell'd to her; but I love thee / By love's own sweet constraint, and will for ever / Do thee all rights of service.
No more of that! Please don't fight against my vows. I was forced into marrying her, but I love you by love's own sweet compulsion, and I'll always serve you in every way.
Ay, so you serve us / Till we serve you; but when you have our roses, / You barely leave our thorns to prick ourselves, / And mock us with our bareness.
Yes, you serve us like that until we give in to you. But when you've had our roses, you leave us only the thorns to prick ourselves, and mock us for being stripped bare.

'Tis not the many oaths that makes the truth, / But the plain single vow that is vow'd true. / What is not holy, that we swear not by, / But take the highest to witness: then, pray you, tell me, / If I should swear by Jove's great attributes / I lov'd you dearly, would you believe my oaths / When I did love you ill? This has no holding, / To swear by him whom I protest to love / That I will work against him. Therefore your oaths / Are words and poor conditions; but unseal'd,— / At least in my opinion.

It isn't a lot of oaths that makes something true, but one simple vow sincerely made. We don't swear by what is not holy, but call on the highest to witness. Then tell me, please: if I swore by all Jove's great powers that I loved you dearly, would you believe my oaths when I was loving you badly? It makes no sense to swear by God, whom I claim to love, that I'll act against him. So your oaths are just words and empty conditions, unsealed, at least in my opinion.

Change it, change it. / Be not so holy-cruel. Love is holy; / And my integrity ne'er knew the crafts / That you do charge men with. Stand no more off, / But give thyself unto my sick desires, / Who then recovers. Say thou art mine, and ever / My love as it begins shall so persever.

Change your mind, change it. Don't be so holy and so cruel. Love is holy, and my honesty never knew the tricks you accuse men of. Don't hold back any more, but give yourself to my sick desires, and then they'll recover. Say you're mine, and my love will always last as it begins.
I see that men make hopes in such a case, / That we'll forsake ourselves. Give me that ring.
I see that in such a case men hope we'll give ourselves up. Give me that ring.
I'll lend it thee, my dear, but have no power / To give it from me.
I'll lend it to you, my dear, but I'm not able to give it away.
It is an honour 'longing to our house, / Bequeathed down from many ancestors, / Which were the greatest obloquy i' the world / In me to lose.
It's an honour belonging to my family, handed down from many ancestors. It would be the greatest disgrace in the world for me to lose it.

Mine honour's such a ring; / My chastity's the jewel of our house, / Bequeathed down from many ancestors, / Which were the greatest obloquy i' the world / In me to lose. Thus your own proper wisdom / Brings in the champion honour on my part / Against your vain assault.

My honour is a ring like that. My chastity is the jewel of my family, handed down from many ancestors. It would be the greatest disgrace in the world for me to lose it. So your own wisdom brings honour in as a champion on my side against your empty attack.
Here, take my ring; / My house, mine honour, yea, my life be thine, / And I'll be bid by thee.
Here, take my ring. My house, my honour, yes, my life are yours, and I'll do whatever you tell me.

When midnight comes, knock at my chamber window; / I'll order take my mother shall not hear. / Now will I charge you in the band of truth, / When you have conquer'd my yet maiden-bed, / Remain there but an hour, nor speak to me. / My reasons are most strong; and you shall know them / When back again this ring shall be deliver'd; / And on your finger in the night, I'll put / Another ring, that what in time proceeds / May token to the future our past deeds. / Adieu till then; then fail not. You have won / A wife of me, though there my hope be done.

When midnight comes, knock at my bedroom window. I'll make sure my mother doesn't hear. Now I'll bind you by your promise of truth: when you have conquered my still virgin bed, stay only an hour and don't speak to me. My reasons are very strong, and you'll learn them when this ring is given back to you. And in the night I'll put another ring on your finger, so that whatever happens later may be a sign to the future of what we did. Goodbye until then. Don't fail. You've won a wife in me, though my hope ends there.
A heaven on earth I have won by wooing thee.
I've won a heaven on earth by wooing you.

For which live long to thank both heaven and me! / You may so in the end. / My mother told me just how he would woo, / As if she sat in's heart. She says all men / Have the like oaths. He had sworn to marry me / When his wife's dead; therefore I'll lie with him / When I am buried. Since Frenchmen are so braid, / Marry that will, I live and die a maid. / Only, in this disguise, I think't no sin / To cozen him that would unjustly win.

May you live long to thank both heaven and me for it! You may do, in the end. My mother told me exactly how he would woo me, as if she were inside his heart. She says all men swear the same oaths. He has sworn to marry me when his wife's dead, so I'll sleep with him when I'm buried. Since Frenchmen are so deceitful, let those who want to marry; I'll live and die a virgin. Only, in this disguise, I don't think it's a sin to cheat a man who would win unfairly.
You have not given him his mother's letter?
You haven't given him his mother's letter?
I have deliv'red it an hour since; there is something in't that stings / his nature; for on the reading it, he chang'd almost into another man.
I delivered it an hour ago. There's something in it that stings him, because when he read it he changed almost into a different man.
He has much worthy blame laid upon him for shaking off so good a wife / and so sweet a lady.
He deserves a lot of the blame he gets for throwing off so good a wife and so sweet a lady.
Especially he hath incurred the everlasting displeasure of the king, / who had even tun'd his bounty to sing happiness to him. I will tell you / a thing, but you shall let it dwell darkly with you.
