Above all he has earned the King's lasting displeasure, when the King had tuned his generosity to sing happiness to him. I'll tell you something, but you must keep it hidden.
When you have spoken it, 'tis dead, and I am the grave of it.
Once you've told me, it's dead, and I'm its grave.

He hath perverted a young gentlewoman here in Florence, of a most / chaste renown, and this night he fleshes his will in the spoil of her / honour; he hath given her his monumental ring, and thinks himself made / in the unchaste composition.

He has corrupted a young gentlewoman here in Florence with a reputation for great chastity, and tonight he satisfies his lust on the spoils of her honour. He has given her his family ring, and thinks he has made a great bargain in this unchaste deal.
Now, God delay our rebellion! As we are ourselves, what things are we!
Now God hold back our sinful nature! Left to ourselves, what creatures we are!

Merely our own traitors. And as in the common course of all treasons, / we still see them reveal themselves till they attain to their abhorr'd / ends; so he that in this action contrives against his own nobility, in / his proper stream, o'erflows himself.

Nothing but traitors to ourselves. And just as we always see treasons reveal themselves before they reach their hateful ends, so he who plots against his own nobility in this action overflows his own banks and drowns himself.
Is it not meant damnable in us to be trumpeters of our unlawful / intents? We shall not then have his company tonight?
Isn't it damnable of us to trumpet our own unlawful plans? So we won't have his company tonight?
Not till after midnight; for he is dieted to his hour.
Not until after midnight, because he's held to his appointment.
That approaches apace. I would gladly have him see his company / anatomized, that he might take a measure of his own judgments, wherein / so curiously he had set this counterfeit.
That's coming fast. I'd love him to see his companion dissected, so that he can measure his own judgement, in which he set such a high value on this fake.
We will not meddle with him till he come; for his presence must be the / whip of the other.
We won't touch Parolles until Bertram comes, because his presence must be the whip for the other.
In the meantime, what hear you of these wars?
Meanwhile, what do you hear about these wars?
I hear there is an overture of peace.
I hear there's an offer of peace.
Nay, I assure you, a peace concluded.
No, I assure you, peace has been agreed.
What will Count Rossillon do then? Will he travel higher, or return / again into France?
What will Count Rossillon do then? Will he travel further, or go back to France?
I perceive by this demand, you are not altogether of his council.
I see from your question that you're not entirely in his confidence.
Let it be forbid, sir! So should I be a great deal of his act.
God forbid, sir! Then I'd have a great share in what he does.

Sir, his wife some two months since fled from his house. Her pretence / is a pilgrimage to Saint Jaques le Grand; which holy undertaking with / most austere sanctimony she accomplished; and there residing, the / tenderness of her nature became as a prey to her grief; in fine, made a / groan of her last breath, and now she sings in heaven.

Sir, his wife ran away from his house about two months ago. She claimed to be going on a pilgrimage to Saint Jaques the Great, and she completed that holy journey with the strictest devotion. While she was staying there, her gentle nature fell prey to her grief. In short, she groaned her last breath, and now she sings in heaven.

The stronger part of it by her own letters, which makes her story true, / even to the point of her death. Her death itself, which could not be / her office to say is come, was faithfully confirm'd by the rector of / the place.
Most of it by her own letters, which tell her story right up to the point of her death. Her death itself, which she couldn't report herself, was reliably confirmed by the priest of the place.
Hath the count all this intelligence?
Does the count know all this?
Ay, and the particular confirmations, point from point, to the full / arming of the verity.
Yes, and all the detailed proofs, point by point, which fully arm the truth.
I am heartily sorry that he'll be glad of this.
I'm truly sorry that he'll be glad about this.
How mightily sometimes we make us comforts of our losses!
How strongly we sometimes make comforts out of our losses!
And how mightily some other times we drown our gain in tears! The great / dignity that his valour hath here acquir'd for him shall at home be / encountered with a shame as ample.
And how strongly at other times we drown our gains in tears! The great honour his courage has won him here will be met at home with an equally great shame.
The web of our life is of a mingled yarn, good and ill together; our / virtues would be proud if our faults whipped them not; and our crimes / would despair if they were not cherish'd by our virtues.
The fabric of our life is woven from mixed thread, good and bad together. Our virtues would be proud if our faults didn't whip them, and our crimes would despair if our virtues didn't comfort them.
He met the duke in the street, sir; of whom he hath taken a solemn / leave: his lordship will next morning for France. The duke hath offered / him letters of commendations to the king.
He met the Duke in the street, sir, and has taken a formal leave of him. His lordship goes to France tomorrow morning. The Duke has offered him letters recommending him to the King.
They shall be no more than needful there, if they were more than they / can commend.
He'll need them there, even if they praised him more than he deserves.
They cannot be too sweet for the king's tartness. Here's his lordship / now. How now, my lord, is't not after midnight?
They can't be too sweet for the King's sour mood. Here's his lordship now. Well, my lord, isn't it past midnight?

I have tonight despatch'd sixteen businesses, a month's length apiece; / by an abstract of success: I have congied with the duke, done my adieu / with his nearest; buried a wife, mourn'd for her, writ to my lady / mother I am returning, entertained my convoy, and between these main / parcels of despatch effected many nicer needs: the last was the / greatest, but that I have not ended yet.

Tonight I have dealt with sixteen pieces of business, each of which would take a month, listed by how they went. I've taken leave of the Duke, said goodbye to those closest to him, buried a wife, mourned for her, written to my lady mother that I'm coming home, arranged my escort, and between these main items done many smaller ones. The last was the most important, but I haven't finished that yet.
If the business be of any difficulty and this morning your departure / hence, it requires haste of your lordship.
If the business is at all difficult and you leave this morning, your lordship will have to hurry.

I mean the business is not ended, as fearing to hear of it hereafter. / But shall we have this dialogue between the Fool and the Soldier? Come, / bring forth this counterfeit module has deceiv'd me like a / double-meaning prophesier.

I mean the business isn't finished, because I'm afraid of hearing about it later. But shall we have this dialogue between the Fool and the Soldier? Come on, bring out this fake model of a soldier who has fooled me like a two-faced prophet.
Has sat i' the stocks all night, poor gallant knave.
He's sat in the stocks all night, the poor dashing rogue.
No matter; his heels have deserv'd it, in usurping his spurs so long. / How does he carry himself?
No matter. His heels have earned it, wearing spurs they had no right to for so long. How is he bearing up?

I have told your lordship already; the stocks carry him. But to answer / you as you would be understood: he weeps like a wench that had shed her / milk; he hath confessed himself to Morgan, whom he supposes to be a / friar, from the time of his remembrance to this very instant disaster / of his setting i' the stocks. And what think you he hath confessed?

I've already told your lordship: the stocks are bearing him up. But to answer you as you mean it: he's crying like a girl who has spilt her milk. He has confessed to Morgan, whom he thinks is a friar, everything from the earliest time he can remember to this present disaster of being put in the stocks. And what do you think he's confessed?
His confession is taken, and it shall be read to his face; if your / lordship be in't, as I believe you are, you must have the patience to / hear it.
His confession has been written down, and it will be read to his face. If your lordship is in it, as I believe you are, you must be patient enough to listen.
A plague upon him! muffled! he can say nothing of me; hush, hush!
Damn him! Blindfolded! He can't say anything about me. Hush, hush!
Here comes blind man's buff! Portotartarossa.
He calls for the tortures. What will you say without 'em?
He's calling for the instruments of torture. What will you say without them?
I will confess what I know without constraint. If ye pinch me like a / pasty I can say no more.
I'll confess what I know without being forced. If you squeezed me like a pie, I couldn't say any more.
You are a merciful general. Our general bids you answer to what I shall / ask you out of a note.
You have a merciful general. Our general orders you to answer what I ask you from a list.
And truly, as I hope to live.
And truthfully, as I hope to live.
'First demand of him how many horse the duke is strong.' What say you / to that?
"First ask him how many cavalry the Duke has." What do you say to that?
Five or six thousand; but very weak and unserviceable: the troops are / all scattered, and the commanders very poor rogues, upon my reputation / and credit, and as I hope to live.
Five or six thousand, but very weak and useless. The troops are all scattered, and the commanders are very poor rogues, on my reputation and credit, and as I hope to live.
Shall I set down your answer so?
Shall I write your answer down like that?
Do. I'll take the sacrament on 't, how and which way you will.
Do. I'll swear it on the sacrament, any way you like.
All's one to him. What a past-saving slave is this!
It's all the same to him. What a hopeless villain this is!

You are deceived, my lord; this is Monsieur Parolles, the gallant / militarist (that was his own phrase), that had the whole theoric of war / in the knot of his scarf, and the practice in the chape of his dagger.

You're mistaken, my lord. This is Monsieur Parolles, the "gallant militarist" (that was his own phrase), who had the whole theory of war in the knot of his scarf and its practice in the tip of his dagger sheath.
I will never trust a man again for keeping his sword clean, nor believe / he can have everything in him by wearing his apparel neatly.
I'll never trust a man again just because he keeps his sword clean, or believe he has every quality because he dresses neatly.
'Five or six thousand horse' I said—I will say true—or thereabouts, set / down,—for I'll speak truth.
"Five or six thousand horse," I said (I'll tell the truth), "or thereabouts." Write it down, because I'll speak the truth.
He's very near the truth in this.
He's very near the truth there.
But I con him no thanks for't in the nature he delivers it.
But I don't thank him for it, the way he tells it.
Poor rogues, I pray you say.
I humbly thank you, sir; a truth's a truth, the rogues are marvellous / poor.
Thank you humbly, sir. A truth's a truth: the rogues are amazingly poor.
'Demand of him of what strength they are a-foot.' What say you to that?
"Ask him how strong the infantry is." What do you say to that?

By my troth, sir, if I were to live this present hour, I will tell / true. Let me see: Spurio, a hundred and fifty, Sebastian, so many; / Corambus, so many; Jaques, so many; Guiltian, Cosmo, Lodowick, and / Gratii, two hundred fifty each; mine own company, Chitopher, Vaumond, / Bentii, two hundred fifty each: so that the muster-file, rotten and / sound, upon my life, amounts not to fifteen thousand poll; half of the / which dare not shake the snow from off their cassocks lest they shake / themselves to pieces.

Honestly, sir, if I had only an hour to live, I'll tell the truth. Let me see: Spurio, a hundred and fifty; Sebastian, the same; Corambus, the same; Jaques, the same; Guiltian, Cosmo, Lodowick and Gratii, two hundred and fifty each; my own company, Chitopher, Vaumond and Bentii, two hundred and fifty each. So the whole muster, rotten and sound, on my life, doesn't come to fifteen thousand heads, and half of them don't dare shake the snow off their cloaks in case they shake themselves to pieces.
What shall be done to him?
What shall be done to him?
Nothing, but let him have thanks. Demand of him my condition, and what / credit I have with the duke.
Nothing, except thank him. Ask him about me, and what standing I have with the Duke.

Well, that's set down. 'You shall demand of him whether one Captain / Dumaine be i' the camp, a Frenchman; what his reputation is with the / duke, what his valour, honesty and expertness in wars; or whether he / thinks it were not possible with well-weighing sums of gold to corrupt / him to a revolt.' What say you to this? What do you know of it?

Well, that's written down. "You shall ask him whether a certain Captain Dumaine, a Frenchman, is in the camp; what his reputation is with the Duke; what his courage, honesty and skill in war are; or whether he thinks it would be possible to bribe him into treason with heavy sums of gold." What do you say to this? What do you know about it?
I beseech you, let me answer to the particular of the inter'gatories. / Demand them singly.
Please, let me answer each of the questions separately. Ask them one at a time.
Do you know this Captain Dumaine?
Do you know this Captain Dumaine?
I know him: he was a botcher's 'prentice in Paris, from whence he was / whipped for getting the shrieve's fool with child, a dumb innocent that / could not say him nay.
I know him. He was a tailor's apprentice in Paris, and was whipped out of there for getting the sheriff's simple-minded girl pregnant, a poor dumb innocent who couldn't say no to him.
Nay, by your leave, hold your hands; though I know his brains are / forfeit to the next tile that falls.
No, if you don't mind, hold your hands, though I know his brains are forfeit to the next tile that falls off a roof.
Well, is this captain in the Duke of Florence's camp?
Well, is this captain in the Duke of Florence's camp?
Upon my knowledge, he is, and lousy.
To my knowledge he is, and covered in lice.
Nay, look not so upon me; we shall hear of your lordship anon.
No, don't look at me like that. We'll hear about your lordship soon.
What is his reputation with the duke?
What is his reputation with the Duke?
The duke knows him for no other but a poor officer of mine, and writ to / me this other day to turn him out o' the band. I think I have his / letter in my pocket.
The Duke knows him only as a poor officer of mine, and wrote to me the other day to throw him out of the company. I think I have his letter in my pocket.
In good sadness, I do not know; either it is there or it is upon a / file, with the duke's other letters, in my tent.
In all seriousness, I don't know. Either it's there, or it's on a file with the Duke's other letters in my tent.
Here 'tis; here's a paper; shall I read it to you?
Here it is. Here's a paper. Shall I read it to you?
I do not know if it be it or no.
I don't know if it's the one or not.
Our interpreter is doing it well.
[Reads] Dian, the Count's a fool, and full of gold.
[Reads] "Diana, the Count's a fool, and full of gold."

That is not the duke's letter, sir; that is an advertisement to a / proper maid in Florence, one Diana, to take heed of the allurement of / one Count Rossillon, a foolish idle boy, but for all that very ruttish. / I pray you, sir, put it up again.

That isn't the Duke's letter, sir. That's a warning to a decent girl in Florence called Diana, to watch out for the temptations of a certain Count Rossillon, a foolish, idle boy, but very lustful all the same. Please, sir, put it away again.
Nay, I'll read it first by your favour.
No, I'll read it first, with your permission.

My meaning in't, I protest, was very honest in the behalf of the maid; / for I knew the young count to be a dangerous and lascivious boy, who is / a whale to virginity, and devours up all the fry it finds.
I swear my purpose in it was very honest, on the girl's behalf, because I knew the young count was a dangerous and lecherous boy, a whale to virginity, who swallows up all the little fish he finds.

[Reads] / When he swears oaths, bid him drop gold, and take it; / After he scores, he never pays the score. / Half won is match well made; match, and well make it; / He ne'er pays after-debts, take it before. / And say a soldier, 'Dian,' told thee this: / Men are to mell with, boys are not to kiss; / For count of this, the count's a fool, I know it, / Who pays before, but not when he does owe it. / Thine, as he vow'd to thee in thine ear, / PAROLLES.

[Reads] "When he swears oaths, tell him to drop gold, and take it. Once he has run up a bill, he never pays it. A bargain half won is a bargain well made; make the bargain, and make it well. He never pays debts afterwards; get paid first. And tell yourself, Diana, a soldier told you this: men are for sleeping with, boys are not to be kissed. Because take note of this: the count's a fool, I know it, who pays in advance but not when he owes. Yours, as he swore to you in your ear, Parolles."
He shall be whipped through the army with this rhyme in's forehead.
He'll be whipped through the army with this rhyme stuck on his forehead.
This is your devoted friend, sir, the manifold linguist, and the / armipotent soldier.
This is your devoted friend, sir, the man of many languages and the mighty soldier.
I could endure anything before but a cat, and now he's a cat to me.
I could put up with anything before except a cat, and now he's a cat to me.
I perceive, sir, by our general's looks we shall be fain to hang you.
I can see from our general's looks, sir, that we'll have to hang you.

My life, sir, in any case. Not that I am afraid to die, but that, my / offences being many, I would repent out the remainder of nature. Let me / live, sir, in a dungeon, i' the stocks, or anywhere, so I may live.

My life, sir, at any cost! Not that I'm afraid to die, but since my sins are many, I'd like to spend the rest of my natural life repenting. Let me live, sir, in a dungeon, in the stocks, anywhere, as long as I live.
We'll see what may be done, so you confess freely. Therefore, once more / to this Captain Dumaine: you have answer'd to his reputation with the / duke, and to his valour. What is his honesty?
We'll see what can be done, as long as you confess freely. So, once more about this Captain Dumaine: you've answered about his reputation with the Duke and his courage. What about his honesty?

He will steal, sir, an egg out of a cloister: for rapes and ravishments / he parallels Nessus. He professes not keeping of oaths; in breaking / them he is stronger than Hercules. He will lie, sir, with such / volubility that you would think truth were a fool: drunkenness is his / best virtue, for he will be swine-drunk, and in his sleep he does / little harm, save to his bedclothes about him; but they know his / conditions and lay him in straw. I have but little more to say, sir, of / his honesty; he has everything that an honest man should not have; what / an honest man should have, he has nothing.

He would steal an egg out of a monastery, sir. For rape and abduction he's the equal of Nessus. He makes a point of not keeping oaths; in breaking them he's stronger than Hercules. He'll lie, sir, so fluently that you'd think truth was a fool. Drunkenness is his best virtue, because he'll get pig-drunk, and in his sleep he does little harm, except to his bedclothes; but they know his habits and lay him on straw. I have little more to say about his honesty, sir: he has everything an honest man shouldn't have, and nothing an honest man should.
I begin to love him for this.
I'm starting to love him for this.
For this description of thine honesty? A pox upon him for me, he's more / and more a cat.
For this description of your honesty? Damn him, as far as I'm concerned he's more and more a cat.
What say you to his expertness in war?
What do you say about his skill in war?

Faith, sir, has led the drum before the English tragedians,—to belie / him I will not,—and more of his soldiership I know not, except in that / country he had the honour to be the officer at a place there called / Mile-end, to instruct for the doubling of files. I would do the man / what honour I can, but of this I am not certain.

Honestly, sir, he has led the drum in front of the English touring actors (I won't lie about him), and I know nothing more of his soldiering, except that in that country he had the honour to be the officer at a place called Mile End, teaching men to march in double file. I'd like to give the man what honour I can, but I'm not sure of this.
He hath out-villain'd villainy so far that the rarity redeems him.
He has outdone villainy so far that his rarity redeems him.
A pox on him! He's a cat still.
Damn him! He's still a cat.
His qualities being at this poor price, I need not to ask you if gold / will corrupt him to revolt.
Since his qualities are so cheap, I needn't ask you if gold would bribe him into treason.
Sir, for a quart d'ecu he will sell the fee-simple of his salvation, / the inheritance of it, and cut the entail from all remainders, and a / perpetual succession for it perpetually.
Sir, for a quarter of a crown he'd sell the freehold of his salvation, the inheritance of it, cut off all future heirs from it, and sell the right of succession to it for ever.
What's his brother, the other Captain Dumaine?
What about his brother, the other Captain Dumaine?
Why does he ask him of me?
Why is he asking him about me?

E'en a crow o' the same nest; not altogether so great as the first in / goodness, but greater a great deal in evil. He excels his brother for a / coward, yet his brother is reputed one of the best that is. In a / retreat he outruns any lackey; marry, in coming on he has the cramp.

Just a crow from the same nest. Not quite as great as the first in goodness, but a great deal greater in evil. He beats his brother as a coward, and yet his brother is thought one of the best cowards there is. In a retreat he outruns any footman, but when it comes to advancing he gets cramp.
If your life be saved, will you undertake to betray the Florentine?
If your life is saved, will you agree to betray the Duke of Florence?
Ay, and the captain of his horse, Count Rossillon.
Yes, and the commander of his cavalry, Count Rossillon.
I'll whisper with the general, and know his pleasure.
I'll whisper with the general and find out what he wants.

[Aside] I'll no more drumming; a plague of all drums! Only to seem / to deserve well, and to beguile the supposition of that lascivious / young boy the count, have I run into this danger: yet who would have / suspected an ambush where I was taken?

[Aside] No more drumming for me. A plague on all drums! Just to seem to deserve well, and to fool that lecherous young boy the count into thinking well of me, I've run into this danger. Yet who would have suspected an ambush where I was caught?

There is no remedy, sir, but you must die. The general says you that / have so traitorously discovered the secrets of your army, and made such / pestiferous reports of men very nobly held, can serve the world for no / honest use; therefore you must die. Come, headsman, off with his head.

There's no help for it, sir: you must die. The general says that you, who have so treacherously revealed your army's secrets and made such poisonous reports about men of very noble reputation, can't be of any honest use to the world. So you must die. Come, executioner, off with his head.
O Lord! sir, let me live, or let me see my death.
Oh Lord, sir! Let me live, or let me see my death.
That shall you, and take your leave of all your friends.
So you shall, and say goodbye to all your friends.
So, look about you; know you any here?
There, look around you. Do you know anyone here?
Captain, what greeting will you to my Lord Lafew? I am for France.
Captain, what message would you like to send to my Lord Lafew? I'm going to France.
Good Captain, will you give me a copy of the sonnet you writ to Diana / in behalf of the Count Rossillon? And I were not a very coward I'd / compel it of you; but fare you well.
Good captain, will you give me a copy of the poem you wrote to Diana for Count Rossillon? If I weren't such a coward I'd force it out of you. But goodbye.
You are undone, captain: all but your scarf; that has a knot on't yet.
You're finished, captain, all except your scarf. That still has a knot in it.
Who cannot be crushed with a plot?
Who couldn't be crushed by a plot?
If you could find out a country where but women were that had received / so much shame, you might begin an impudent nation. Fare ye well, sir. I / am for France too; we shall speak of you there.
If you could find a country where only women lived who had suffered so much shame, you could start a shameless nation. Goodbye, sir. I'm going to France too. We'll talk about you there.

Yet am I thankful. If my heart were great / 'Twould burst at this. Captain I'll be no more, / But I will eat, and drink, and sleep as soft / As captain shall. Simply the thing I am / Shall make me live. Who knows himself a braggart, / Let him fear this; for it will come to pass / That every braggart shall be found an ass. / Rust, sword; cool, blushes; and, Parolles live / Safest in shame; being fool'd, by foolery thrive. / There's place and means for every man alive. / I'll after them.

Still, I'm thankful. If my heart were proud, this would make it burst. I'll be a captain no more, but I'll eat and drink and sleep as comfortably as any captain. Simply being what I am will keep me alive. Anyone who knows he's a braggart, let him fear this, because it will come to pass that every braggart is found out to be an ass. Rust, sword; cool down, blushes; and, Parolles, live safest in shame. Having been made a fool of, prosper by foolery. There's a place and a living for every man alive. I'll go after them.

That you may well perceive I have not wrong'd you / One of the greatest in the Christian world / Shall be my surety; fore whose throne 'tis needful, / Ere I can perfect mine intents, to kneel. / Time was I did him a desired office, / Dear almost as his life; which gratitude / Through flinty Tartar's bosom would peep forth, / And answer thanks. I duly am inform'd / His grace is at Marseilles; to which place / We have convenient convoy. You must know / I am supposed dead. The army breaking, / My husband hies him home, where, heaven aiding, / And by the leave of my good lord the king, / We'll be before our welcome.

So that you can see clearly I haven't wronged you, one of the greatest men in the Christian world will guarantee my word. Before I can complete my plans, I must kneel before his throne. Once I did him a service he longed for, almost as dear to him as his life. Gratitude for that would show itself even through the stony heart of a Tartar and answer with thanks. I'm reliably told his majesty is at Marseilles, and we have a convenient escort there. You must know that I'm thought to be dead. Now the army is breaking up, my husband is hurrying home, where, with heaven's help and the permission of my good lord the King, we'll arrive before we're expected.
Gentle madam, / You never had a servant to whose trust / Your business was more welcome.
Gentle madam, you never had a servant who was more glad to be trusted with your business.

Nor you, mistress, / Ever a friend whose thoughts more truly labour / To recompense your love. Doubt not but heaven / Hath brought me up to be your daughter's dower, / As it hath fated her to be my motive / And helper to a husband. But, O strange men! / That can such sweet use make of what they hate, / When saucy trusting of the cozen'd thoughts / Defiles the pitchy night; so lust doth play / With what it loathes, for that which is away. / But more of this hereafter. You, Diana, / Under my poor instructions yet must suffer / Something in my behalf.

Nor, mistress, did you ever have a friend whose thoughts worked harder to repay your love. Don't doubt that heaven has raised me up to provide your daughter's dowry, just as it has destined her to be my means and my helper to a husband. But oh, strange men, who can make such sweet use of what they hate, when the lustful trust of their deceived thoughts stains the pitch-black night! So lust plays with what it loathes, in place of what is absent. But more of this later. You, Diana, must still put up with something more for my sake, under my poor instructions.
Let death and honesty / Go with your impositions, I am yours / Upon your will to suffer.
As long as death and chastity go along with what you ask of me, I'm yours to suffer as you wish.

Yet, I pray you; / But with the word the time will bring on summer, / When briers shall have leaves as well as thorns, / And be as sweet as sharp. We must away; / Our waggon is prepar'd, and time revives us. / All's well that ends well; still the fine's the crown. / Whate'er the course, the end is the renown.

Wait a little more, I beg you. With time, summer will come, when briars will have leaves as well as thorns, and be as sweet as they are sharp. We must go. Our carriage is ready, and time calls us on. All's well that ends well; the ending is always the crown. Whatever the route, it's the end that brings the glory.

No, no, no, your son was misled with a snipt-taffeta fellow there, / whose villanous saffron would have made all the unbak'd and doughy / youth of a nation in his colour. Your daughter-in-law had been alive at / this hour, and your son here at home, more advanc'd by the king than by / that red-tail'd humble-bee I speak of.

No, no, no, your son was led astray by a fellow in slashed silk over there, whose wicked yellow would have dyed all the half-baked, doughy young men of a nation his colour. Your daughter-in-law would be alive at this moment, and your son here at home, promoted further by the King, if it weren't for that red-tailed bumblebee I'm talking about.

I would I had not known him; it was the death of the most virtuous / gentlewoman that ever nature had praise for creating. If she had / partaken of my flesh and cost me the dearest groans of a mother, I / could not have owed her a more rooted love.

I wish I'd never known him. He was the death of the most virtuous young woman nature was ever praised for creating. If she had been my own flesh and blood and cost me a mother's dearest groans in childbirth, I couldn't have loved her more deeply.
'Twas a good lady, 'twas a good lady. We may pick a thousand salads ere / we light on such another herb.
She was a good lady, she was a good lady. We could pick a thousand salads before we came across another herb like her.
Indeed, sir, she was the sweet marjoram of the salad, or, rather, the / herb of grace.
Indeed, sir, she was the sweet marjoram of the salad, or rather the herb of grace.
They are not herbs, you knave; they are nose-herbs.
They're not salad herbs, you rogue; they're herbs for smelling.
I am no great Nebuchadnezzar, sir; I have not much skill in grass.
I'm no great Nebuchadnezzar, sir. I don't know much about grass.
Whether dost thou profess thyself,—a knave or a fool?
Which do you claim to be, a rogue or a fool?
A fool, sir, at a woman's service, and a knave at a man's.
A fool, sir, in a woman's service, and a rogue in a man's.
I would cozen the man of his wife, and do his service.
I'd cheat the man of his wife, and do his job for him.
So you were a knave at his service indeed.
Then you'd be a rogue in his service indeed.
And I would give his wife my bauble, sir, to do her service.
And I'd give his wife my fool's stick, sir, to do her service.
I will subscribe for thee; thou art both knave and fool.
I'll vouch for you: you're both rogue and fool.
Why, sir, if I cannot serve you, I can serve as great a prince as you / are.
Why, sir, if I can't serve you, I can serve as great a prince as you are.
Faith, sir, 'a has an English name; but his phisnomy is more hotter in / France than there.
Well, sir, he has an English name, but his face burns hotter in France than in England.
The black prince, sir; alias the prince of darkness; alias the devil.
The Black Prince, sir, otherwise known as the Prince of Darkness, otherwise known as the devil.
Hold thee, there's my purse. I give thee not this to suggest thee from / thy master thou talk'st of; serve him still.
Wait, here's my purse. I'm not giving you this to tempt you away from that master you talk about. Go on serving him.

I am a woodland fellow, sir, that always loved a great fire, and the / master I speak of ever keeps a good fire. But sure he is the prince of / the world; let his nobility remain in's court. I am for the house with / the narrow gate, which I take to be too little for pomp to enter: some / that humble themselves may, but the many will be too chill and tender, / and they'll be for the flow'ry way that leads to the broad gate and the / great fire.

I'm a country fellow, sir, who always loved a big fire, and the master I'm talking about always keeps a good fire. But surely he's the prince of this world; let his nobles stay at his court. I'm for the house with the narrow gate, which I think is too small for pomp to get through. Some who humble themselves may, but most will be too chilly and soft, and they'll go for the flowery path that leads to the wide gate and the great fire.
Go thy ways, I begin to be a-weary of thee; and I tell thee so before, / because I would not fall out with thee. Go thy ways; let my horses be / well look'd to, without any tricks.

Off you go. I'm beginning to get tired of you, and I'm telling you so in advance because I don't want to quarrel with you. Off you go, and make sure my horses are well looked after, without any tricks.
If I put any tricks upon 'em, sir, they shall be jades' tricks, which / are their own right by the law of nature.
If I play any tricks on them, sir, they'll be horse tricks, which they have a right to by the law of nature.
A shrewd knave, and an unhappy.
A sharp rogue, and a mischievous one.

So he is. My lord that's gone made himself much sport out of him; by / his authority he remains here, which he thinks is a patent for his / sauciness; and indeed he has no pace, but runs where he will.

So he is. My late husband used to have great fun with him. He stays here because my husband wanted it, and he thinks that gives him a licence for his cheek. In fact he keeps no proper pace, but runs wherever he likes.

I like him well; 'tis not amiss. And I was about to tell you, since I / heard of the good lady's death, and that my lord your son was upon his / return home, I moved the king my master to speak in the behalf of my / daughter; which, in the minority of them both, his majesty out of a / self-gracious remembrance did first propose. His highness hath promis'd / me to do it; and, to stop up the displeasure he hath conceived against / your son, there is no fitter matter. How does your ladyship like it?

I like him very much; there's no harm in him. I was about to tell you: since I heard of the good lady's death, and that my lord your son was on his way home, I asked the King my master to speak on behalf of my daughter, a match his majesty himself first proposed, out of his own kindness, when they were both children. His highness has promised me to do it, and there's no better way to settle the displeasure he has felt against your son. How does your ladyship like it?
With very much content, my lord, and I wish it happily effected.
Very much, my lord, and I hope it happily comes about.
His highness comes post from Marseilles, of as able body as when he / number'd thirty; he will be here tomorrow, or I am deceived by him that / in such intelligence hath seldom fail'd.
His highness is riding fast from Marseilles, as healthy as when he was thirty. He'll be here tomorrow, or I'm misled by a man who has rarely been wrong in such news.
It rejoices me that I hope I shall see him ere I die. I have letters / that my son will be here tonight. I shall beseech your lordship to / remain with me till they meet together.
I'm glad that I may hope to see him before I die. I have letters saying my son will be here tonight. I beg your lordship to stay with me until they meet.
Madam, I was thinking with what manners I might safely be admitted.
Madam, I was wondering how I could politely be allowed to stay.
You need but plead your honourable privilege.
You need only claim your honourable privilege.
Lady, of that I have made a bold charter; but, I thank my God, it holds / yet.
Lady, I've made bold use of that privilege, but, thank God, it still holds.

O madam, yonder's my lord your son with a patch of velvet on's face; / whether there be a scar under't or no, the velvet knows; but 'tis a / goodly patch of velvet. His left cheek is a cheek of two pile and a / half, but his right cheek is worn bare.

Oh, madam, there's my lord your son over there with a patch of velvet on his face. Whether there's a scar under it or not, the velvet knows, but it's a fine patch of velvet. His left cheek is two-and-a-half-pile velvet, but his right cheek is worn bare.
A scar nobly got, or a noble scar, is a good livery of honour; so / belike is that.
A scar nobly won, or a noble scar, is a fine uniform of honour, and that's probably one.
But it is your carbonado'd face.
But it's a face slashed like a grilled steak.
Let us go see your son, I pray you. I long to talk with the young noble / soldier.
Let's go and see your son, please. I long to talk with the noble young soldier.
Faith, there's a dozen of 'em, with delicate fine hats, and most / courteous feathers, which bow the head and nod at every man.
Honestly, there are a dozen of them, with delicate fine hats and the politest feathers, which bow their heads and nod at everyone.

But this exceeding posting day and night / Must wear your spirits low. We cannot help it. / But since you have made the days and nights as one, / To wear your gentle limbs in my affairs, / Be bold you do so grow in my requital / As nothing can unroot you. In happy time;—

But this extreme rushing day and night must be wearing you out. We can't help it. But since you have made days and nights the same, wearing out your gentle bodies in my affairs, be sure you are growing so firmly in my gratitude that nothing can uproot you. Just at the right moment...
This man may help me to his majesty's ear, / If he would spend his power. God save you, sir.
This man may help me to get the King to listen, if he would use his influence. God save you, sir.
Sir, I have seen you in the court of France.
Sir, I have seen you at the French court.

I do presume, sir, that you are not fallen / From the report that goes upon your goodness; / And therefore, goaded with most sharp occasions, / Which lay nice manners by, I put you to / The use of your own virtues, for the which / I shall continue thankful.

I take it, sir, that you haven't fallen short of your reputation for goodness. So, driven by very urgent circumstances that push aside polite manners, I call on you to use your own virtues, and I'll be grateful to you for it.
That it will please you / To give this poor petition to the king, / And aid me with that store of power you have / To come into his presence.
That you will be kind enough to give this humble petition to the King, and use what influence you have to help me come before him.
Not indeed. / He hence remov'd last night, and with more haste / Than is his use.
Not indeed. He left here last night, and in more of a hurry than usual.
Lord, how we lose our pains!
Lord, how our efforts are wasted!
All's well that ends well yet, / Though time seem so adverse and means unfit. / I do beseech you, whither is he gone?
All's well that ends well still, though time seems so against us and our means so unsuitable. Please, where has he gone?
Marry, as I take it, to Rossillon; / Whither I am going.
Well, as I understand it, to Rossillon, where I'm going.

I do beseech you, sir, / Since you are like to see the king before me, / Commend the paper to his gracious hand, / Which I presume shall render you no blame, / But rather make you thank your pains for it. / I will come after you with what good speed / Our means will make us means.

I beg you, sir, since you are likely to see the King before me, put this paper into his gracious hand. I'm sure it will bring you no blame, but rather make you glad you took the trouble. I'll follow you as fast as our means allow.
And you shall find yourself to be well thank'd, / Whate'er falls more. We must to horse again. / Go, go, provide.
And you'll find yourself well thanked, whatever else happens. We must get on our horses again. Go, go, get ready.

Good Monsieur Lavache, give my Lord Lafew this letter; I have ere now, / sir, been better known to you, when I have held familiarity with / fresher clothes; but I am now, sir, muddied in Fortune's mood, and / smell somewhat strong of her strong displeasure.

Good Monsieur Lavatch, give my Lord Lafew this letter. In the past, sir, you knew me better, when I wore fresher clothes. But now, sir, I've been muddied in Fortune's moat, and smell rather strongly of her strong displeasure.
Truly, Fortune's displeasure is but sluttish, if it smell so strongly / as thou speak'st of. I will henceforth eat no fish of Fortune's / buttering. Pr'ythee, allow the wind.
Honestly, Fortune's displeasure must be filthy if it smells as strongly as you say. From now on I'll eat no fish cooked in Fortune's butter. Please, stand downwind.
Nay, you need not to stop your nose, sir. I spake but by a metaphor.
No, you needn't hold your nose, sir. I was only speaking in a metaphor.
Indeed, sir, if your metaphor stink, I will stop my nose, or against / any man's metaphor. Pr'ythee, get thee further.
Indeed, sir, if your metaphor stinks, I'll hold my nose, as I would against any man's metaphor. Please, get further away.
Pray you, sir, deliver me this paper.
Please, sir, deliver this paper for me.
Foh, pr'ythee stand away. A paper from Fortune's close-stool to give to / a nobleman! Look here he comes himself.
Pah! Please, stand back. A paper from Fortune's toilet to give to a nobleman! Look, here he comes himself.

Here is a pur of Fortune's, sir, or of Fortune's cat, but not a / musk-cat, that has fallen into the unclean fishpond of her displeasure, / and as he says, is muddied withal. Pray you, sir, use the carp as you / may, for he looks like a poor, decayed, ingenious, foolish, rascally / knave. I do pity his distress in my similes of comfort, and leave him / to your lordship.

Here's one of Fortune's purrs, sir, or one of Fortune's cats (but not a musk-cat), who has fallen into the dirty fishpond of her displeasure and, as he says, is muddied with it. Please, sir, treat this carp as you can, because he looks like a poor, ruined, clever, foolish, rascally rogue. I pity his distress with my comforting comparisons, and leave him to your lordship.
My lord, I am a man whom Fortune hath cruelly scratch'd.
My lord, I am a man whom Fortune has cruelly scratched.

And what would you have me to do? 'Tis too late to pare her nails now. / Wherein have you played the knave with Fortune that she should scratch / you, who of herself is a good lady, and would not have knaves thrive / long under her? There's a quart d'ecu for you. Let the justices make / you and Fortune friends; I am for other business.

And what do you want me to do? It's too late to cut her nails now. How have you played the rogue with Fortune that she should scratch you, when she's a good lady herself and won't let rogues prosper under her for long? There's a quarter crown for you. Let the magistrates make you and Fortune friends; I have other business.
I beseech your honour to hear me one single word.
I beg your honour to hear me say one single word.
You beg a single penny more. Come, you shall ha't; save your word.
You're begging one single penny more. Come on, you shall have it; save your word.
My name, my good lord, is Parolles.
My name, my good lord, is Parolles.
You beg more than word then. Cox my passion! Give me your hand. How / does your drum?
Then you're begging for more than one word. God's passion! Give me your hand. How's your drum?
O my good lord, you were the first that found me.
Oh, my good lord, you were the first who found me out.
Was I, in sooth? And I was the first that lost thee.
Was I, really? And I was the first who lost you.
It lies in you, my lord, to bring me in some grace, for you did bring / me out.
It's in your power, my lord, to bring me back into favour, since you brought me out of it.
Out upon thee, knave! dost thou put upon me at once both the office of / God and the devil? One brings thee in grace, and the other brings thee / out.
Shame on you, rogue! Do you give me the jobs of both God and the devil at once? One brings you into grace, and the other brings you out.
The king's coming; I know by his trumpets. Sirrah, inquire further / after me. I had talk of you last night; though you are a fool and a / knave, you shall eat. Go to; follow.
The King's coming; I can tell by his trumpets. Fellow, come and see me later. I was talking about you last night. Though you're a fool and a rogue, you shall eat. Go on, follow me.
We lost a jewel of her, and our esteem / Was made much poorer by it; but your son, / As mad in folly, lack'd the sense to know / Her estimation home.
We lost a jewel in her, and our worth was made much poorer by it. But your son, mad in his folly, didn't have the sense to understand her full value.
'Tis past, my liege, / And I beseech your majesty to make it / Natural rebellion, done i' the blaze of youth, / When oil and fire, too strong for reason's force, / O'erbears it and burns on.
It's past, my lord, and I beg your majesty to treat it as natural rebellion, done in the heat of youth, when passion, like oil and fire, is too strong for reason, overpowers it and burns on.
My honour'd lady, / I have forgiven and forgotten all, / Though my revenges were high bent upon him, / And watch'd the time to shoot.
My honoured lady, I have forgiven and forgotten everything, though my revenge was aimed high at him and waited for the moment to shoot.

This I must say,— / But first, I beg my pardon,—the young lord / Did to his majesty, his mother, and his lady, / Offence of mighty note; but to himself / The greatest wrong of all. He lost a wife / Whose beauty did astonish the survey / Of richest eyes; whose words all ears took captive; / Whose dear perfection hearts that scorn'd to serve / Humbly call'd mistress.

I must say this (but first I beg your pardon): the young lord did great wrong to his majesty, his mother and his wife, but the greatest wrong of all to himself. He lost a wife whose beauty amazed the most experienced eyes, whose words captivated every ear, and whose precious perfection made hearts too proud to serve humbly call her mistress.

Praising what is lost / Makes the remembrance dear. Well, call him hither; / We are reconcil'd, and the first view shall kill / All repetition. Let him not ask our pardon; / The nature of his great offence is dead, / And deeper than oblivion do we bury / Th' incensing relics of it. Let him approach / A stranger, no offender; and inform him / So 'tis our will he should.

Praising what is lost makes the memory precious. Well, call him here. We are reconciled, and the first sight of him will put an end to going over it again. He mustn't ask our pardon. His great offence is dead, and we bury its angering remains deeper than forgetfulness. Let him come to us as a stranger, not an offender, and tell him that is our wish.
What says he to your daughter? Have you spoke?
What does he say about your daughter? Have you spoken?
All that he is hath reference to your highness.
Everything about him is at your highness's command.
Then shall we have a match. I have letters sent me / That sets him high in fame.
Then we'll have a match. I've been sent letters that speak very highly of him.
I am not a day of season, / For thou mayst see a sunshine and a hail / In me at once. But to the brightest beams / Distracted clouds give way; so stand thou forth; / The time is fair again.
I'm not a day of one season, because you can see sunshine and hail in me at once. But scattered clouds give way to the brightest rays, so step forward. The weather is fine again.
My high-repented blames / Dear sovereign, pardon to me.
Dear sovereign, forgive me the faults I deeply repent.

All is whole. / Not one word more of the consumed time. / Let's take the instant by the forward top; / For we are old, and on our quick'st decrees / Th'inaudible and noiseless foot of time / Steals ere we can effect them. You remember / The daughter of this lord?

All is mended. Not one more word about the time that's gone. Let's seize the moment by the forelock, because we are old, and the silent, noiseless foot of time creeps up on our quickest decisions before we can carry them out. You remember this lord's daughter?

Admiringly, my liege. At first / I stuck my choice upon her, ere my heart / Durst make too bold herald of my tongue: / Where the impression of mine eye infixing, / Contempt his scornful perspective did lend me, / Which warp'd the line of every other favour, / Scorn'd a fair colour, or express'd it stolen, / Extended or contracted all proportions / To a most hideous object. Thence it came / That she whom all men prais'd, and whom myself, / Since I have lost, have lov'd, was in mine eye / The dust that did offend it.

With admiration, my lord. I fixed my choice on her at first, before my heart dared send my tongue out as too bold a messenger. When her image was fixed in my eye, Contempt lent me his scornful lens, which twisted the shape of every other face, scorned a fair complexion or claimed it was painted, and stretched or shrank all proportions into a hideous object. That's how it came about that she whom all men praised, and whom I myself have loved since I lost her, was to my eye the speck of dust that hurt it.

Well excus'd: / That thou didst love her, strikes some scores away / From the great compt: but love that comes too late, / Like a remorseful pardon slowly carried, / To the great sender turns a sour offence, / Crying, That's good that's gone. Our rash faults / Make trivial price of serious things we have, / Not knowing them until we know their grave. / Oft our displeasures, to ourselves unjust, / Destroy our friends, and after weep their dust: / Our own love waking cries to see what's done, / While shameful hate sleeps out the afternoon. / Be this sweet Helen's knell, and now forget her. / Send forth your amorous token for fair Maudlin. / The main consents are had, and here we'll stay / To see our widower's second marriage-day.

Well excused. That you did love her cancels some of the great debt. But love that comes too late, like a pardon brought slowly and with regret, turns into a bitter offence against the great one who sent it, crying, "What's gone was good." Our rash faults put a low price on the serious things we have, not knowing their worth until we know their grave. Often our anger, unjust to ourselves, destroys our friends, and afterwards we weep over their dust. Our own love wakes and weeps to see what's been done, while shameful hate sleeps through the afternoon. Let this be sweet Helen's funeral bell, and now forget her. Send your love token to fair Maudlin. The main agreements have been made, and we'll stay here to see our widower's second wedding day.
Which better than the first, O dear heaven, bless! / Or, ere they meet, in me, O nature, cesse!
Dear heaven, bless it better than the first! Or, before they come together, let nature stop in me!
Come on, my son, in whom my house's name / Must be digested; give a favour from you, / To sparkle in the spirits of my daughter, / That she may quickly come.
Come on, my son, into whom my family's name must be absorbed. Give a love token from you to sparkle in my daughter's spirits, so that she comes quickly.
By my old beard, / And ev'ry hair that's on 't, Helen that's dead / Was a sweet creature: such a ring as this, / The last that e'er I took her leave at court, / I saw upon her finger.
By my old beard and every hair on it, Helen, who is dead, was a sweet creature. I saw a ring like this on her finger the last time I said goodbye to her at court.

Now, pray you, let me see it; for mine eye, / While I was speaking, oft was fasten'd to it. / This ring was mine; and when I gave it Helen / I bade her, if her fortunes ever stood / Necessitied to help, that by this token / I would relieve her. Had you that craft to 'reave her / Of what should stead her most?

Now, please let me see it, because while I was speaking my eye was often fixed on it. This ring was mine, and when I gave it to Helen I told her that if she ever needed help, I would help her if she sent this token. Were you so cunning as to rob her of what would help her most?
My gracious sovereign, / Howe'er it pleases you to take it so, / The ring was never hers.
My gracious sovereign, however you choose to take it, the ring was never hers.
Son, on my life, / I have seen her wear it; and she reckon'd it / At her life's rate.
Son, on my life, I have seen her wear it, and she valued it as highly as her life.
I am sure I saw her wear it.
I'm sure I saw her wear it.

You are deceiv'd, my lord; she never saw it. / In Florence was it from a casement thrown me, / Wrapp'd in a paper, which contain'd the name / Of her that threw it. Noble she was, and thought / I stood engag'd; but when I had subscrib'd / To mine own fortune, and inform'd her fully / I could not answer in that course of honour / As she had made the overture, she ceas'd, / In heavy satisfaction, and would never / Receive the ring again.

You're mistaken, my lord: she never saw it. In Florence it was thrown to me from a window, wrapped in a paper with the name of the woman who threw it. She was noble, and thought I was free to marry. But when I had explained my situation and told her fully that I couldn't respond honourably to the offer she had made, she gave up, sadly accepting it, and would never take the ring back.

Plutus himself, / That knows the tinct and multiplying medicine, / Hath not in nature's mystery more science / Than I have in this ring. 'Twas mine, 'twas Helen's, / Whoever gave it you. Then if you know / That you are well acquainted with yourself, / Confess 'twas hers, and by what rough enforcement / You got it from her. She call'd the saints to surety / That she would never put it from her finger / Unless she gave it to yourself in bed, / Where you have never come, or sent it us / Upon her great disaster.

Plutus himself, who knows the secret of turning metal to gold, doesn't understand nature's mysteries better than I know this ring. It was mine, it was Helen's, whoever gave it to you. So if you know yourself at all, confess that it was hers, and by what brutal force you got it from her. She called on the saints to witness that she would never take it off her finger unless she gave it to you yourself in bed (where you have never been), or sent it to us in some great disaster.

Thou speak'st it falsely, as I love mine honour, / And mak'st conjectural fears to come into me / Which I would fain shut out. If it should prove / That thou art so inhuman,—'twill not prove so: / And yet I know not, thou didst hate her deadly. / And she is dead; which nothing but to close / Her eyes myself, could win me to believe / More than to see this ring. Take him away.

You're lying, as surely as I love my honour, and you put fearful suspicions into my mind that I'd gladly shut out. If it should turn out that you are so inhuman... it won't turn out like that. And yet I don't know: you hated her mortally. And she is dead, and nothing but closing her eyes myself could convince me of it more than seeing this ring. Take him away.
My fore-past proofs, howe'er the matter fall, / Shall tax my fears of little vanity, / Having vainly fear'd too little. Away with him. / We'll sift this matter further.
My earlier evidence, however this turns out, will clear my fears of being foolish, since I was foolish to fear too little. Away with him. We'll look into this further.
If you shall prove / This ring was ever hers, you shall as easy / Prove that I husbanded her bed in Florence, / Where she yet never was.
If you can prove this ring was ever hers, you can just as easily prove that I slept with her as her husband in Florence, where she never was.
I am wrapp'd in dismal thinkings.

Gracious sovereign, / Whether I have been to blame or no, I know not: / Here's a petition from a Florentine, / Who hath for four or five removes come short / To tender it herself. I undertook it, / Vanquish'd thereto by the fair grace and speech / Of the poor suppliant, who by this, I know, / Is here attending: her business looks in her / With an importing visage, and she told me / In a sweet verbal brief, it did concern / Your highness with herself.

Gracious sovereign, I don't know whether I've done wrong or not. Here's a petition from a Florentine woman who has missed you at four or five stops on the way and so couldn't hand it to you herself. I took it on, won over by the poor petitioner's grace and speech. I know she is here by now, waiting. Her business shows in her face as something urgent, and she told me in a sweet short speech that it concerned your highness and herself.

[Reads] Upon his many protestations to marry me when his wife was / dead, I blush to say it, he won me. Now is the Count Rossillon a / widower; his vows are forfeited to me, and my honour's paid to him. He / stole from Florence, taking no leave, and I follow him to his country / for justice. Grant it me, O king, in you it best lies; otherwise a / seducer flourishes, and a poor maid is undone. / DIANA CAPILET.

[Reads] "Because he swore so many times to marry me when his wife was dead, I blush to say it, he won me. Now the Count of Rossillon is a widower: his vows are owed to me, and my honour has been paid to him. He slipped away from Florence without saying goodbye, and I follow him to his country for justice. Grant it to me, O King; it is most in your power. Otherwise a seducer prospers and a poor girl is ruined. Diana Capilet."
I will buy me a son-in-law in a fair, and toll for this. I'll none of / him.
I'll buy myself a son-in-law at a fair and pay the market toll for him. I'll have none of this one.
The heavens have thought well on thee, Lafew, / To bring forth this discovery. Seek these suitors. / Go speedily, and bring again the count.
The heavens have favoured you, Lafew, by bringing this discovery to light. Find these petitioners. Go quickly, and bring the count back again.
I am afeard the life of Helen, lady, / Was foully snatch'd.
I'm afraid, lady, that Helen's life was foully taken.
Then justice on those who did it!
I wonder, sir, since wives are monsters to you, / And that you fly them as you swear them lordship, / Yet you desire to marry. What woman's that?
I wonder, sir, since wives are monsters to you and you run away from them as soon as you swear to be their husband, that you still want to marry. Who is that woman?
I am, my lord, a wretched Florentine, / Derived from the ancient Capilet; / My suit, as I do understand, you know, / And therefore know how far I may be pitied.
I am, my lord, a wretched Florentine, descended from the ancient Capilet family. I understand you know what I'm asking for, and so you know how much I deserve pity.
I am her mother, sir, whose age and honour / Both suffer under this complaint we bring, / And both shall cease, without your remedy.
I'm her mother, sir. My age and my honour both suffer from this complaint we bring, and both will die unless you put it right.
Come hither, count; do you know these women?
Come here, Count. Do you know these women?
My lord, I neither can nor will deny / But that I know them. Do they charge me further?
My lord, I can't and won't deny that I know them. Do they accuse me of anything more?
Why do you look so strange upon your wife?
Why do you look at your wife as if she were a stranger?
She's none of mine, my lord.
She's no wife of mine, my lord.

If you shall marry, / You give away this hand, and that is mine, / You give away heaven's vows, and those are mine, / You give away myself, which is known mine; / For I by vow am so embodied yours / That she which marries you must marry me, / Either both or none.

If you marry, you give away this hand, and that is mine; you give away vows made to heaven, and those are mine; you give away me, who am known to be yours. Because by your vow I am so made one with you that whoever marries you must marry me: both of us or neither.
[To Bertram] Your reputation comes too short for my daughter; you are / no husband for her.
[To Bertram] Your reputation falls too short for my daughter. You're no husband for her.
My lord, this is a fond and desperate creature / Whom sometime I have laugh'd with. Let your highness / Lay a more noble thought upon mine honour / Than for to think that I would sink it here.
My lord, this is a foolish, desperate creature I've sometimes laughed with. Let your highness think more nobly of my honour than to believe I'd sink it so low.
Sir, for my thoughts, you have them ill to friend / Till your deeds gain them; fairer prove your honour / Than in my thought it lies!
Sir, as for my thoughts, they won't be your friends until your actions win them. May your honour prove better than I now think it!
Good my lord, / Ask him upon his oath, if he does think / He had not my virginity.
My good lord, ask him on his oath whether he doesn't think he took my virginity.
What do you say to her?
She's impudent, my lord, / And was a common gamester to the camp.
She's shameless, my lord, and was a common whore to the army.

He does me wrong, my lord; if I were so / He might have bought me at a common price. / Do not believe him. O, behold this ring, / Whose high respect and rich validity / Did lack a parallel; yet for all that / He gave it to a commoner o' the camp, / If I be one.

He wrongs me, my lord. If I were, he could have bought me at the common price. Don't believe him. Oh, look at this ring, whose high value and rich worth had no equal. And yet he gave it to a common woman of the camp, if that's what I am.
He blushes, and 'tis it. / Of six preceding ancestors, that gem / Conferr'd by testament to th' sequent issue, / Hath it been owed and worn. This is his wife; / That ring's a thousand proofs.
He's blushing, and it's the ring. That jewel has been owned and worn by six ancestors, each leaving it in his will to the next heir. This is his wife. That ring is a thousand proofs.
Methought you said / You saw one here in court could witness it.
I thought you said you saw someone here at court who could witness it.
I did, my lord, but loath am to produce / So bad an instrument; his name's Parolles.
I did, my lord, but I'm reluctant to bring forward such a bad instrument. His name's Parolles.
I saw the man today, if man he be.
I saw the man today, if he is a man.
Find him, and bring him hither.
Find him and bring him here.

What of him? / He's quoted for a most perfidious slave, / With all the spots o' the world tax'd and debauch'd: / Whose nature sickens but to speak a truth. / Am I or that or this for what he'll utter, / That will speak anything?

What about him? He's known as a most treacherous slave, accused of and corrupted by every stain in the world, whose nature is sickened by just speaking a truth. Am I to be judged this or that by what he says, when he'll say anything?
She hath that ring of yours.
She has that ring of yours.

I think she has. Certain it is I lik'd her / And boarded her i' the wanton way of youth. / She knew her distance, and did angle for me, / Madding my eagerness with her restraint, / As all impediments in fancy's course / Are motives of more fancy; and in fine, / Her infinite cunning with her modern grace, / Subdu'd me to her rate; she got the ring, / And I had that which any inferior might / At market-price have bought.

I think she has. It's true that I liked her and made advances to her in the reckless way of youth. She knew how to keep her distance, and fished for me, maddening my eagerness with her restraint, since every obstacle in the course of desire makes desire stronger. In the end her endless cunning, with her ordinary charms, brought me down to her price. She got the ring, and I got what any lower man could have bought at the market price.

I must be patient. / You that have turn'd off a first so noble wife / May justly diet me. I pray you yet,— / Since you lack virtue, I will lose a husband— / Send for your ring, I will return it home, / And give me mine again.

I must be patient. You, who turned off a first wife so noble, may well starve me too. Still, I ask you (since you lack virtue, I'll lose a husband): send for your ring, I'll give it back, and give me mine again.
What ring was yours, I pray you?
Which ring was yours, may I ask?
Sir, much like / The same upon your finger.
Sir, very like the one on your finger.
Know you this ring? This ring was his of late.
Do you know this ring? This ring was his until just now.
And this was it I gave him, being abed.
And that's the one I gave him, in bed.
The story then goes false you threw it him / Out of a casement.
Then the story that you threw it to him out of a window is false.
My lord, I do confess the ring was hers.
My lord, I confess the ring was hers.
You boggle shrewdly; every feather starts you. / Is this the man you speak of?
You shy badly; every feather startles you. Is this the man you spoke of?
Tell me, sirrah, but tell me true I charge you, / Not fearing the displeasure of your master, / Which on your just proceeding, I'll keep off,— / By him and by this woman here what know you?
Tell me, fellow, but tell me the truth, I order you, without fearing your master's anger, which I'll keep off you if you behave honestly: what do you know about him and this woman here?
So please your majesty, my master hath been an honourable gentleman. / Tricks he hath had in him, which gentlemen have.
If it please your majesty, my master has been an honourable gentleman. He has had tricks in him, as gentlemen do.
Come, come, to the purpose. Did he love this woman?
Come, come, to the point. Did he love this woman?
Faith, sir, he did love her; but how?
Well, sir, he did love her; but how?
He did love her, sir, as a gentleman loves a woman.
He loved her, sir, as a gentleman loves a woman.
He lov'd her, sir, and lov'd her not.
He loved her, sir, and didn't love her.
As thou art a knave and no knave. / What an equivocal companion is this!
Just as you're a rogue and not a rogue. What a slippery fellow this is!
I am a poor man, and at your majesty's command.
I'm a poor man, and at your majesty's command.
He's a good drum, my lord, but a naughty orator.
He's a good drum, my lord, but a bad speaker.
Do you know he promised me marriage?
Do you know he promised to marry me?
Faith, I know more than I'll speak.
Honestly, I know more than I'll say.
But wilt thou not speak all thou know'st?
But won't you say all you know?

Yes, so please your majesty. I did go between them as I said; but more / than that, he loved her, for indeed he was mad for her, and talked of / Satan, and of Limbo, and of furies, and I know not what: yet I was in / that credit with them at that time that I knew of their going to bed; / and of other motions, as promising her marriage, and things which would / derive me ill will to speak of; therefore I will not speak what I know.

Yes, if your majesty pleases. I did go between them, as I said, but more than that, he loved her, because indeed he was mad about her, and talked of Satan and Limbo and the Furies and I don't know what. Yet I was so trusted by them at that time that I knew about their going to bed, and other moves, such as promising to marry her, and things that would earn me ill will if I spoke of them. So I won't say what I know.
Thou hast spoken all already, unless thou canst say they are married; / but thou art too fine in thy evidence; therefore stand aside. This / ring, you say, was yours?
You've said everything already, unless you can say they're married. But you're too clever in your evidence, so stand aside. You say this ring was yours?
Where did you buy it? Or who gave it you?
Where did you buy it? Or who gave it to you?
It was not given me, nor I did not buy it.
It wasn't given to me, and I didn't buy it.
It was not lent me neither.
It wasn't lent to me either.
Where did you find it then?
Where did you find it, then?
If it were yours by none of all these ways, / How could you give it him?
If it wasn't yours by any of these ways, how could you give it to him?
I never gave it to him.
This woman's an easy glove, my lord; she goes off and on at pleasure.
This woman is a loose glove, my lord: she slips off and on as she pleases.
This ring was mine, I gave it his first wife.
This ring was mine. I gave it to his first wife.
It might be yours or hers for ought I know.
It might be yours or hers, for all I know.
Take her away, I do not like her now. / To prison with her. And away with him. / Unless thou tell'st me where thou hadst this ring, / Thou diest within this hour.
Take her away. I don't like her now. To prison with her. And take him away too. Unless you tell me where you got this ring, you'll die within the hour.
I'll put in bail, my liege.
I'll put up bail, my lord.
I think thee now some common customer.
Now I think you're some common prostitute.
By Jove, if ever I knew man, 'twas you.
By Jove, if I ever slept with a man, it was you.
Wherefore hast thou accus'd him all this while?
Then why have you accused him all this time?

Because he's guilty, and he is not guilty. / He knows I am no maid, and he'll swear to't: / I'll swear I am a maid, and he knows not. / Great King, I am no strumpet, by my life; / I am either maid, or else this old man's wife.

Because he's guilty, and he's not guilty. He knows I'm not a virgin, and he'll swear to it. I'll swear I am a virgin, and he doesn't know. Great King, I'm no whore, on my life. I'm either a virgin or else this old man's wife.
She does abuse our ears; to prison with her.
She's playing with our ears. To prison with her.
Good mother, fetch my bail. Stay, royal sir;
Good mother, fetch my bail. Wait, royal sir.

The jeweller that owes the ring is sent for, / And he shall surety me. But for this lord / Who hath abus'd me as he knows himself, / Though yet he never harm'd me, here I quit him. / He knows himself my bed he hath defil'd; / And at that time he got his wife with child. / Dead though she be, she feels her young one kick; / So there's my riddle: one that's dead is quick, / And now behold the meaning.

The jeweller who owns the ring has been sent for, and he'll vouch for me. But as for this lord, who has wronged me, as he knows himself, though he never actually harmed me, here I let him off. He thinks he has defiled my bed, and at that very time he got his wife pregnant. Though she's dead, she feels her baby kick. So there's my riddle: someone dead is alive. And now see the answer.
Is there no exorcist / Beguiles the truer office of mine eyes? / Is't real that I see?
Is there some magician deceiving my eyes? Is what I'm seeing real?
No, my good lord; / 'Tis but the shadow of a wife you see, / The name, and not the thing.
No, my good lord. It's only the shadow of a wife you see: the name, and not the thing.

O, my good lord, when I was like this maid; / I found you wondrous kind. There is your ring, / And, look you, here's your letter. This it says, / 'When from my finger you can get this ring, / And is by me with child, &c.' This is done; / Will you be mine now you are doubly won?

Oh, my good lord, when I was taking this girl's place, I found you wonderfully kind. There's your ring, and look, here's your letter. It says, "When you can get this ring from my finger, and are pregnant by me..." and so on. This is done. Will you be mine now that you've been won twice over?
If she, my liege, can make me know this clearly, / I'll love her dearly, ever, ever dearly.
If she can make me understand this clearly, my lord, I'll love her dearly, for ever, for ever dearly.
If it appear not plain, and prove untrue, / Deadly divorce step between me and you! / O my dear mother, do I see you living?
If it isn't made plain and proves untrue, let deadly divorce come between you and me! Oh, my dear mother, do I see you alive?

Mine eyes smell onions; I shall weep anon. / [To Parolles] Good Tom Drum, lend me a handkercher. / So, I thank thee. Wait on me home, I'll make sport with thee. / Let thy courtesies alone, they are scurvy ones.

My eyes smell onions; I'll be crying in a minute. [To Parolles] Good Tom Drum, lend me a handkerchief. So, thank you. Come home with me; I'll have some fun with you. Never mind your bowing and scraping; it's a sorry business.

Let us from point to point this story know, / To make the even truth in pleasure flow. / [To Diana] If thou beest yet a fresh uncropped flower, / Choose thou thy husband, and I'll pay thy dower; / For I can guess that by thy honest aid, / Thou kept'st a wife herself, thyself a maid. / Of that and all the progress more and less, / Resolvedly more leisure shall express. / All yet seems well, and if it end so meet, / The bitter past, more welcome is the sweet.

Let us hear this story point by point, so that the plain truth can flow with pleasure. [To Diana] If you are still a fresh, unpicked flower, choose your husband, and I'll pay your dowry, because I can guess that by your honest help you kept a wife a wife and yourself a virgin. Of that, and of everything that happened, great and small, we'll hear in full when there's more time. All still seems well, and if it ends so fittingly, the bitter past makes the sweet more welcome.

The king's a beggar, now the play is done; / All is well ended if this suit be won, / That you express content; which we will pay / With strife to please you, day exceeding day. / Ours be your patience then, and yours our parts; / Your gentle hands lend us, and take our hearts.

The King is a beggar, now that the play is over. All has ended well if we win this request: that you show you are satisfied. We will repay you by striving to please you, more every day. So let us have your patience, and you take our parts. Lend us your gentle hands in applause, and take our hearts.
